**Tafsir of Surat Fatir**

It is Meccan. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Duraysh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Surat Fatir was revealed in Mecca.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

Al-fatr (splitting open) means cleaving something. It is said: "I split it (fatartuhu) and it split (infatara)." From this comes "the camel's tooth split (fatara naab al-ba'ir)" when it emerged, so it is called "a camel that has split its tooth (ba'ir fatir)." Tafattara al-shay' means the thing cracked. Al-fatr also means initiating and originating, and this is the meaning intended here. The meaning is: "All praise is due to Allah, the Originator and Creator of the heavens and the earth." The purpose of this is that whoever is able to initiate this great creation is able to bring it back.

The majority of reciters (al-jumhur) read *fatir* in the active participle form. Al-Zuhri and al-Dahhak read *fatara* in the past tense form. According to the first reading, it is a qualifier (na't) of Allah. Its annexation (idafa) is definite (mahda) because it carries the meaning of the past tense. If the annexation were not definite, it would be a substitute (badal). The same applies to ﴿جاعِلِ المَلائِكَةِ رُسُلًا﴾ (the Maker of the angels as messengers), where both possibilities are allowed. According to the first reading, *rusulan* (as messengers) is in the accusative by an implied verb, because the active participle does not govern when it carries the meaning of the past tense. Al-Kisa'i permitted its governing.

According to the second reading, *rusulan* is in the accusative governed by *jai'il* (Maker). The messengers from among the angels are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Izra'il.

Al-Hasan read *jai'ilu* with a nominative ending (raf'). Khalil ibn Nashit and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *ja'ala* in the past tense form.

Al-Hasan and Humayd read *rusulan* with a sukun on the sin (*rusl*), which is the dialect of Tamim. ﴿أولي أجنحة﴾ (possessors of wings) is a qualifier of *rusulan*. *Ajniha* is the plural of *janah* (wing). ﴿مثنى وثلاث ورباع﴾ (two, three, and four) is a qualifier of *ajniha*. The discussion of *mathna wa thulatha wa ruba'* has already been covered in *al-Nisa'*.

Qatada said: some of them have two wings, some have three, and some have four. They descend with them from the heaven to the earth and ascend with them from the earth to the heaven.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: Allah sends them to the prophets.

Al-Suddi said: to the servants, with His blessings or His punishments.

The clause ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾ (He adds to creation what He wills) is a resumptive sentence (mustanaffa), confirming what precedes it regarding the differing states of the angels. The meaning is that He adds to the creation of the angels whatever He wills. This is the view of most exegetes, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred it. It has also been said that this addition to creation is not restricted to the angels. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Juraij said it is beautiful voice.

Qatada said: it is attractiveness in the eyes, beauty in the nose, and sweetness in the mouth. It has also been said: a beautiful face; it has been said: beautiful handwriting; it has been said: curly hair; it has been said: intellect and discernment; it has been said: knowledge and crafts. There is no basis for restricting this to a specific type, rather it includes every addition. The clause ﴿إن الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ (Indeed Allah is over all things competent) is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, that He ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾.

﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah grants to mankind, none can withhold it). That is, whatever rain and provision Allah brings them, no one can withhold it, and whatever He withholds from that, no one can release it after He has withheld it. It has also been said: the meaning is that the messengers were sent as a mercy to mankind, so none other than Allah can send them. It has been said: it means supplication. It has been said: it means repentance. It has been said: it means divine success and guidance.

There is no basis for this restriction. Rather the meaning is: whatever Allah opens to mankind from the treasures of His mercy, it includes every blessing with which Allah bestows His creation. Likewise, withholding includes everything Allah withholds from His blessings. He, glory be to Him, is the Giver, the Withholder, the Constrictor and the Expander; there is no giver other than Him and no bestower other than Him.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His servants to remember His blessings, which overflow upon them and which cannot be counted or enumerated: ﴿وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها﴾ (If you counted the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them) [Ibrahim: 34]. The meaning of this command to remember is to guide them to gratitude, to preserve those blessings and to seek more of them.

﴿هل من خالق غير الله﴾ (Is there any creator other than Allah?). Here *min* is redundant (za'ida), *khaliq* is the subject (mubtada'), and *ghayr Allah* is its qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: *ghayr* is in the nominative because the meaning is "Is there a creator other than Allah?", since *min* is an emphasizing redundant particle. Whoever reads *ghayr* in the genitive treats it as a qualifier according to the wording.

The majority of reciters read *ghayr* in the nominative. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive. Al-Fadl ibn Ibrahim read it in the accusative as an exception (istithna'). The clause ﴿يرزقكم من السماء والأرض﴾ (who provides for you from the heaven and the earth) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject, or a resumptive sentence, or another qualifier of *khaliq*, and its predicate is omitted. Provision from the heaven is by rain, and from the earth is by plants and other things. The clause ﴿لا إله إلا هو﴾ (there is no deity but Him) is a resumptive sentence confirming the negation implied by the interrogative. ﴿فأنى تؤفكون﴾ (How then are you deluded?) comes from *al-afk* with a fatha, which means turning away. It is said: "What turned you away from such-and-such?" meaning "What diverted you?" So: "How are you diverted?" It has also been said that it is derived from *al-ifk* with a kasra, meaning lying, because it is turned away from truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, from where does falsehood and denial of the oneness of Allah and of the resurrection come to you, while you acknowledge that Allah created you and provided for you?

Then Allah, glory be to Him, consoled His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, saying: ﴿وإن يكذبوك فقد كذبت رسل من قبلك﴾ (If they deny you, messengers before you were also denied), so that he may take comfort in those prophets who came before him and be consoled regarding the denial of the Meccan disbelievers. ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾ (And to Allah all matters are returned) and not to anyone else, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Ibn Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Watthab, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *turja'* with a fatha on the *ta'* (the second letter), in the active voice. The rest read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

﴿يا أيها الناس إن وعد الله حق﴾ (O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true). That is, His promise of resurrection, gathering, reckoning, punishment, Paradise and Hellfire, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾. So let not the life of this world deceive you with its adornment and its pleasures. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the deception of the life of this world is that a person becomes preoccupied with its pleasures and delights instead of the deeds of the Hereafter, until he says: ﴿يا ليتني قدمت لحياتي﴾ (Would that I had sent forth for my life) [al-Fajr: 24]. ﴿ولا يغرنكم بالله الغرور﴾ (Nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah). The majority read *al-ghurur* with a fatha on the *ghayn*, meaning the one who greatly deceives, and this is Satan.

Ibn al-Sikkit and Abu Hatim said: *al-Ghurur* is Satan. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj considered this unlikely, because *gharra bihi* is transitive, and the verbal noun of a transitive verb is typically of the form *fa'l*, as in *darabahu darban*, except for a few well-known exceptions that are not used as a basis for analogy. The meaning of the verse is: do not let Satan deceive you about Allah, so that he tells you that Allah will overlook your sins and forgive you because of your merit or because of the vastness of His mercy toward you.

Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read *al-ghurur* with a damma on the *ghayn*, meaning falsehood.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: *al-ghurur* with a damma is what deceives of the goods of this world.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ghurur* may be the plural of *gharr* (deceiver), like *qa'id* and *qu'ud*. It has been said: it may also be a verbal noun of *gharrahu*, like *al-lizum* and *al-nuhuk*, but against this is what al-Zajjaj said about its unlikelihood.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, warned His servants about Satan, saying: ﴿إن الشيطان لكم عدو فاتخذوه عدوا﴾ (Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy). That is, oppose him by obeying Allah, and do not obey him in acts of disobedience to Allah.

Then He explained to His servants the manner of Satan's enmity toward them, saying: ﴿إنما يدعو حزبه ليكونوا من أصحاب السعير﴾ (He only invites his party so that they become companions of the Blaze). That is, he only calls his followers, his adherents and those who obey him to acts of disobedience to Allah, glory be to Him, so that they become people of the Fire.

The relative clause in ﴿الذين كفروا لهم عذاب شديد﴾ (Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment) may be in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿لهم عذاب شديد﴾ as its predicate. It may be in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the subject of *yakunu* (they become). It may be in the accusative as a substitute for *hizbahu*, or as a qualifier of it, or by an implied verb indicating blame. It may be in the genitive as a substitute for *ashab* or as a qualifier of it. The nominative as the subject is the strongest of these possibilities, because after mentioning Satan's enmity and his calling of his party, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the two groups: those who obey him and those who disobey Allah. The first group has a severe punishment, and the other group is described in ﴿والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ (But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward). That is, Allah will forgive them because of their faith and righteous deeds, and will give them a great reward, which is Paradise.

﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا﴾ (Is one to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive so that he sees it as good...?). This sentence is a resumptive sentence confirming the difference previously mentioned between the two groups. *Man* is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Kisa'i said: the implied meaning is "his soul has gone out after them in regrets" (*dhahabat nafsuka 'alayhim hasarat*).

He said: this is indicated by His saying: ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ (So do not let yourself go in regret over them). He said: this is a beautiful Arabic expression that only a few know.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied meaning is "like one whom He guided," and others estimated it as "like one who was not made to see his deed as attractive." This latter is better, because it agrees with the wording and the meaning. The author of *al-Kashshaf* erred: he attributed to al-Zajjaj what al-Kisa'i had said.

Al-Nahhas said: what al-Kisa'i said is the best of what has been said about the verse, because of the indication it gives of the omitted element. The meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, from extreme grief over them and sorrow for them, as He said: ﴿فلعلك باخع نفسك﴾ (Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief) [al-Kahf: 6].

The clause ﴿فإن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء﴾ (For indeed Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills) confirms what precedes it, that is: He sends astray whomever He wills to send astray, and guides whomever He wills to guide.

﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ The majority read *tadhhab* with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'*, with *nafsuka* as the subject, so it is of the type of *la uraynaka hahuna* (where the grammatical construction is similar).

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Ashhab read it with a damma on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'*, with *nafsaka* in the accusative. *Hasarat* in the accusative is a causal object (*'illa*), meaning "for the regrets." It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), as if all of it had become regrets because of the intensity of the sorrow, as has been reported from Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad said it is a specifier (*tamyiz*).

*Al-hasra* is the intensity of grief over what has passed.

﴿إن الله عليم بما يصنعون﴾ (Indeed Allah is Knowing of what they do). Nothing among their actions and sayings is hidden from Him. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, together with what it contains of a severe threat.

Abu Ubayd in *Fada'ilihi*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I did not know what *Fatir al-samawat wa al-ard* meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said: "I am the one who *fatartuha*," meaning: "I initiated it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: *Fatir al-samawat* means *Badi' al-samawat* (the Originator of the heavens).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, regarding ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾, that he said: it is the beautiful voice.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: what Allah opens for mankind of the door of repentance, none can withhold; they repent if they wish or if they refuse. What He withholds of the door of repentance, none can release after Him, and they do not repent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated regarding the verse: (p-1206) he said: it means, "You have no part in the matter."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij regarding ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ that he said: every instance in the Qur'an of ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ and ﴿رزق كريم﴾ (a generous provision) refers to Paradise.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada and al-Hasan regarding ﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله﴾ that they said: Satan made it attractive to them, and by Allah, these are misguidances. ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ means: do not grieve over them.

It has also been said that it is derived from *al-ifk* with a kasra, meaning lying, because it is turned away from truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, from where does falsehood and denial of the oneness of Allah and of the resurrection come to you, while you acknowledge that Allah created you and provided for you?

Then Allah, glory be to Him, consoled His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, saying: ﴿وإن يكذبوك فقد كذبت رسل من قبلك﴾ (If they deny you, messengers before you were also denied), so that he may take comfort in those prophets who came before him and be consoled regarding the denial of the Meccan disbelievers. ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾ (And to Allah all matters are returned) and not to anyone else, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Ibn Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Watthab, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *turja'* with a fatha on the *ta'* (the second letter), in the active voice. The rest read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

﴿يا أيها الناس إن وعد الله حق﴾ (O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true). That is, His promise of resurrection, gathering, reckoning, punishment, Paradise and Hellfire, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾. So let not the life of this world deceive you with its adornment and its pleasures. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the deception of the life of this world is that a person becomes preoccupied with its pleasures and delights instead of the deeds of the Hereafter, until he says: ﴿يا ليتني قدمت لحياتي﴾ (Would that I had sent forth for my life) [al-Fajr: 24]. ﴿ولا يغرنكم بالله الغرور﴾ (Nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah). The majority read *al-ghurur* with a fatha on the *ghayn*, meaning the one who greatly deceives, and this is Satan.

Ibn al-Sikkit and Abu Hatim said: *al-Ghurur* is Satan. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj considered this unlikely, because *gharra bihi* is transitive, and the verbal noun of a transitive verb is typically of the form *fa'l*, as in *darabahu darban*, except for a few well-known exceptions that are not used as a basis for analogy. The meaning of the verse is: do not let Satan deceive you about Allah, so that he tells you that Allah will overlook your sins and forgive you because of your merit or because of the vastness of His mercy toward you.

Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read *al-ghurur* with a damma on the *ghayn*, meaning falsehood.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: *al-ghurur* with a damma is what deceives of the goods of this world.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ghurur* may be the plural of *gharr* (deceiver), like *qa'id* and *qu'ud*. It has been said: it may also be a verbal noun of *gharrahu*, like *al-lizum* and *al-nuhuk*, but against this is what al-Zajjaj said about its unlikelihood.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, warned His servants about Satan, saying: ﴿إن الشيطان لكم عدو فاتخذوه عدوا﴾ (Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy). That is, oppose him by obeying Allah, and do not obey him in acts of disobedience to Allah.

Then He explained to His servants the manner of Satan's enmity toward them, saying: ﴿إنما يدعو حزبه ليكونوا من أصحاب السعير﴾ (He only invites his party so that they become companions of the Blaze). That is, he only calls his followers, his adherents and those who obey him to acts of disobedience to Allah, glory be to Him, so that they become people of the Fire.

The relative clause in ﴿الذين كفروا لهم عذاب شديد﴾ (Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment) may be in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿لهم عذاب شديد﴾ as its predicate. It may be in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the subject of *yakunu* (they become). It may be in the accusative as a substitute for *hizbahu*, or as a qualifier of it, or by an implied verb indicating blame. It may be in the genitive as a substitute for *ashab* or as a qualifier of it. The nominative as the subject is the strongest of these possibilities, because after mentioning Satan's enmity and his calling of his party, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the two groups: those who obey him and those who disobey Allah. The first group has a severe punishment, and the other group is described in ﴿والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ (But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward). That is, Allah will forgive them because of their faith and righteous deeds, and will give them a great reward, which is Paradise.

﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا﴾ (Is one to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive so that he sees it as good...?). This sentence is a resumptive sentence confirming the difference previously mentioned between the two groups. *Man* is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Kisa'i said: the implied meaning is "his soul has gone out after them in regrets" (*dhahabat nafsuka 'alayhim hasarat*).

He said: this is indicated by His saying: ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ (So do not let yourself go in regret over them). He said: this is a beautiful Arabic expression that only a few know.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied meaning is "like one whom He guided," and others estimated it as "like one who was not made to see his deed as attractive." This latter is better, because it agrees with the wording and the meaning. The author of *al-Kashshaf* erred: he attributed to al-Zajjaj what al-Kisa'i had said.

Al-Nahhas said: what al-Kisa'i said is the best of what has been said about the verse, because of the indication it gives of the omitted element. The meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, from extreme grief over them and sorrow for them, as He said: ﴿فلعلك باخع نفسك﴾ (Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief) [al-Kahf: 6].

Al-Mubarrad said it is a specifier (*tamyiz*).

*Al-hasra* is the intensity of grief over what has passed.

﴿إن الله عليم بما يصنعون﴾ (Indeed Allah is Knowing of what they do). Nothing among their actions and sayings is hidden from Him. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, together with what it contains of a severe threat.

Abu Ubayd in *Fada'ilihi*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I did not know what *Fatir al-samawat wa al-ard* meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said: "I am the one who *fatartuha*," meaning: "I initiated it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: *Fatir al-samawat* means *Badi' al-samawat* (the Originator of the heavens).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, regarding ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾, that he said: it is the beautiful voice.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: what Allah opens for mankind of the door of repentance, none can withhold; they repent if they wish or if they refuse. What He withholds of the door of repentance, none can release after Him, and they do not repent.

According to the first reading, *rusulan* (as messengers) is in the accusative by an implied verb, because the active participle does not govern when it carries the meaning of the past tense. Al-Kisa'i permitted its governing.

According to the second reading, *rusulan* is in the accusative governed by *jai'il* (Maker). The messengers from among the angels are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Izra'il.

Al-Hasan read *jai'ilu* with a nominative ending (raf'). Khalil ibn Nashit and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *ja'ala* in the past tense form.

The discussion of *mathna wa thulatha wa ruba'* has already been covered in *al-Nisa'*.

Qatada said: some of them have two wings, some have three, and some have four. They descend with them from the heaven to the earth and ascend with them from the earth to the heaven.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: Allah sends them to the prophets.

Al-Suddi said: to the servants, with His blessings or His punishments.

The clause ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾ (He adds to creation what He wills) is a resumptive sentence (mustanaffa), confirming what precedes it regarding the differing states of the angels. The meaning is that He adds to the creation of the angels whatever He wills. This is the view of most exegetes, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred it. It has also been said that this addition to creation is not restricted to the angels. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Juraij said it is beautiful voice.

Qatada said: it is attractiveness in the eyes, beauty in the nose, and sweetness in the mouth. It has also been said: a beautiful face; it has been said: beautiful handwriting; it has been said: curly hair; it has been said: intellect and discernment; it has been said: knowledge and crafts. There is no basis for restricting this to a specific type, rather it includes every addition. The clause ﴿إن الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ (Indeed Allah is over all things competent) is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, that He ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾.

﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah grants to mankind, none can withhold it). That is, whatever rain and provision Allah brings them, no one can withhold it, and whatever He withholds from that, no one can release it after He has withheld it. It has also been said: the meaning is that the messengers were sent as a mercy to mankind, so none other than Allah can send them. It has been said: it means supplication. It has been said: it means repentance. It has been said: it means divine success and guidance.

There is no basis for this restriction. Rather the meaning is: whatever Allah opens to mankind from the treasures of His mercy, it includes every blessing with which Allah bestows His creation. Likewise, withholding includes everything Allah withholds from His blessings. He, glory be to Him, is the Giver, the Withholder, the Constrictor and the Expander; there is no giver other than Him and no bestower other than Him.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His servants to remember His blessings, which overflow upon them and which cannot be counted or enumerated: ﴿وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها﴾ (If you counted the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them) [Ibrahim: 34]. The meaning of this command to remember is to guide them to gratitude, to preserve those blessings and to seek more of them.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: Allah sends them to the prophets.

Al-Suddi said: to the servants, with His blessings or His punishments.

﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah grants to mankind, none can withhold it). It has also been said: the meaning is that the messengers were sent as a mercy to mankind, so none other than Allah can send them. It has been said: it means supplication. It has been said: it means repentance. It has been said: it means divine success and guidance.

Likewise, withholding includes everything Allah withholds from His blessings. Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His servants to remember His blessings, which overflow upon them and which cannot be counted or enumerated: ﴿وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها﴾ (If you counted the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them) [Ibrahim: 34]. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, from where does falsehood and denial of the oneness of Allah and of the resurrection come to you, while you acknowledge that Allah created you and provided for you?

Then Allah, glory be to Him, consoled His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, saying: ﴿وإن يكذبوك فقد كذبت رسل من قبلك﴾ (If they deny you, messengers before you were also denied), so that he may take comfort in those prophets who came before him and be consoled regarding the denial of the Meccan disbelievers. ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾ (And to Allah all matters are returned) and not to anyone else, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

That is, His promise of resurrection, gathering, reckoning, punishment, Paradise and Hellfire, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾. So let not the life of this world deceive you with its adornment and its pleasures. The majority read *al-ghurur* with a fatha on the *ghayn*, meaning the one who greatly deceives, and this is Satan.

Ibn al-Sikkit and Abu Hatim said: *al-Ghurur* is Satan. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj considered this unlikely, because *gharra bihi* is transitive, and the verbal noun of a transitive verb is typically of the form *fa'l*, as in *darabahu darban*, except for a few well-known exceptions that are not used as a basis for analogy. Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read *al-ghurur* with a damma on the *ghayn*, meaning falsehood.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, warned His servants about Satan, saying: ﴿إن الشيطان لكم عدو فاتخذوه عدوا﴾ (Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy). That is, oppose him by obeying Allah, and do not obey him in acts of disobedience to Allah.

Then He explained to His servants the manner of Satan's enmity toward them, saying: ﴿إنما يدعو حزبه ليكونوا من أصحاب السعير﴾ (He only invites his party so that they become companions of the Blaze). That is, he only calls his followers, his adherents and those who obey him to acts of disobedience to Allah, glory be to Him, so that they become people of the Fire.

It may be in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the subject of *yakunu* (they become). It may be in the accusative as a substitute for *hizbahu*, or as a qualifier of it, or by an implied verb indicating blame. It may be in the genitive as a substitute for *ashab* or as a qualifier of it. The nominative as the subject is the strongest of these possibilities, because after mentioning Satan's enmity and his calling of his party, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the two groups: those who obey him and those who disobey Allah. The first group has a severe punishment, and the other group is described in ﴿والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ (But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward). That is, Allah will forgive them because of their faith and righteous deeds, and will give them a great reward, which is Paradise.

This sentence is a resumptive sentence confirming the difference previously mentioned between the two groups. *Man* is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Kisa'i said: the implied meaning is "his soul has gone out after them in regrets" (*dhahabat nafsuka 'alayhim hasarat*).

He said: this is indicated by His saying: ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ (So do not let yourself go in regret over them). He said: this is a beautiful Arabic expression that only a few know.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied meaning is "like one whom He guided," and others estimated it as "like one who was not made to see his deed as attractive." This latter is better, because it agrees with the wording and the meaning. The author of *al-Kashshaf* erred: he attributed to al-Zajjaj what al-Kisa'i had said.

The meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, from extreme grief over them and sorrow for them, as He said: ﴿فلعلك باخع نفسك﴾ (Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief) [al-Kahf: 6].

The clause ﴿فإن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء﴾ (For indeed Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills) confirms what precedes it, that is: He sends astray whomever He wills to send astray, and guides whomever He wills to guide.

﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ The majority read *tadhhab* with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'*, with *nafsuka* as the subject, so it is of the type of *la uraynaka hahuna* (where the grammatical construction is similar).

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Ashhab read it with a damma on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'*, with *nafsaka* in the accusative. *Hasarat* in the accusative is a causal object (*'illa*), meaning "for the regrets." It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), as if all of it had become regrets because of the intensity of the sorrow, as has been reported from Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad said it is a specifier (*tamyiz*).

*Al-hasra* is the intensity of grief over what has passed.

﴿إن الله عليم بما يصنعون﴾ (Indeed Allah is Knowing of what they do). Nothing among their actions and sayings is hidden from Him. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, together with what it contains of a severe threat.

Abu Ubayd in *Fada'ilihi*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I did not know what *Fatir al-samawat wa al-ard* meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said: "I am the one who *fatartuha*," meaning: "I initiated it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: *Fatir al-samawat* means *Badi' al-samawat* (the Originator of the heavens).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, regarding ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾, that he said: it is the beautiful voice.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: what Allah opens for mankind of the door of repentance, none can withhold; they repent if they wish or if they refuse. What He withholds of the door of repentance, none can release after Him, and they do not repent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated regarding the verse: (p-1206) he said: it means, "You have no part in the matter."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij regarding ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ that he said: every instance in the Qur'an of ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ and ﴿رزق كريم﴾ (a generous provision) refers to Paradise.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada and al-Hasan regarding ﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله﴾ that they said: Satan made it attractive to them, and by Allah, these are misguidances. ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ means: do not grieve over them.

**Tafsir of Surat Fatir**

It is Meccan. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Duraysh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Surat Fatir was revealed in Mecca.

The meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, from extreme grief over them and sorrow for them, as He said: ﴿فلعلك باخع نفسك﴾ (Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief) [al-Kahf: 6].

The clause ﴿فإن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء﴾ (For indeed Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills) confirms what precedes it, that is: He sends astray whomever He wills to send astray, and guides whomever He wills to guide.

﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ The majority read *tadhhab* with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'*, with *nafsuka* as the subject, so it is of the type of *la uraynaka hahuna* (where the grammatical construction is similar).

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Ashhab read it with a damma on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'*, with *nafsaka* in the accusative. *Hasarat* in the accusative is a causal object (*'illa*), meaning "for the regrets." It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*), as if all of it had become regrets because of the intensity of the sorrow, as has been reported from Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad said it is a specifier (*tamyiz*).

*Al-hasra* is the intensity of grief over what has passed.

﴿إن الله عليم بما يصنعون﴾ (Indeed Allah is Knowing of what they do). Nothing among their actions and sayings is hidden from Him. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, together with what it contains of a severe threat.

Abu Ubayd in *Fada'ilihi*, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I did not know what *Fatir al-samawat wa al-ard* meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said: "I am the one who *fatartuha*," meaning: "I initiated it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: *Fatir al-samawat* means *Badi' al-samawat* (the Originator of the heavens).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, regarding ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾, that he said: it is the beautiful voice.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: what Allah opens for mankind of the door of repentance, none can withhold; they repent if they wish or if they refuse. What He withholds of the door of repentance, none can release after Him, and they do not repent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated regarding the verse: (p-1206) he said: it means, "You have no part in the matter."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij regarding ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ that he said: every instance in the Qur'an of ﴿لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ and ﴿رزق كريم﴾ (a generous provision) refers to Paradise.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada and al-Hasan regarding ﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله﴾ that they said: Satan made it attractive to them, and by Allah, these are misguidances. ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ means: do not grieve over them.

**Tafsir of Surat Fatir**

It is Meccan. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Duraysh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Surat Fatir was revealed in Mecca.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

Al-fatr (splitting open) means cleaving something. It is said: "I split it (fatartuhu) and it split (infatara)." From this comes "the camel's tooth split (fatara naab al-ba'ir)" when it emerged, so it is called "a camel that has split its tooth (ba'ir fatir)." Tafattara al-shay' means the thing cracked. Al-fatr also means initiating and originating, and this is the meaning intended here. The meaning is: "All praise is due to Allah, the Originator and Creator of the heavens and the earth." The purpose of this is that whoever is able to initiate this great creation is able to bring it back.

The majority of reciters (al-jumhur) read *fatir* in the active participle form. Al-Zuhri and al-Dahhak read *fatara* in the past tense form. According to the first reading, it is a qualifier (na't) of Allah. Its annexation (idafa) is definite (mahda) because it carries the meaning of the past tense. If the annexation were not definite, it would be a substitute (badal). The same applies to ﴿جاعِلِ المَلائِكَةِ رُسُلًا﴾ (the Maker of the angels as messengers), where both possibilities are allowed. According to the first reading, *rusulan* (as messengers) is in the accusative by an implied verb, because the active participle does not govern when it carries the meaning of the past tense. Al-Kisa'i permitted its governing.

According to the second reading, *rusulan* is in the accusative governed by *jai'il* (Maker). The messengers from among the angels are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Izra'il.

Al-Hasan read *jai'ilu* with a nominative ending (raf'). Khalil ibn Nashit and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *ja'ala* in the past tense form.

Al-Hasan and Humayd read *rusulan* with a sukun on the sin (*rusl*), which is the dialect of Tamim. ﴿أولي أجنحة﴾ (possessors of wings) is a qualifier of *rusulan*. *Ajniha* is the plural of *janah* (wing). ﴿مثنى وثلاث ورباع﴾ (two, three, and four) is a qualifier of *ajniha*. The discussion of *mathna wa thulatha wa ruba'* has already been covered in *al-Nisa'*.

Qatada said: some of them have two wings, some have three, and some have four. They descend with them from the heaven to the earth and ascend with them from the earth to the heaven.

Yahya ibn Sallam said: Allah sends them to the prophets.

Al-Suddi said: to the servants, with His blessings or His punishments.

The clause ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾ (He adds to creation what He wills) is a resumptive sentence (mustanaffa), confirming what precedes it regarding the differing states of the angels. The meaning is that He adds to the creation of the angels whatever He wills. This is the view of most exegetes, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj preferred it. It has also been said that this addition to creation is not restricted to the angels. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Juraij said it is beautiful voice.

Qatada said: it is attractiveness in the eyes, beauty in the nose, and sweetness in the mouth. It has also been said: a beautiful face; it has been said: beautiful handwriting; it has been said: curly hair; it has been said: intellect and discernment; it has been said: knowledge and crafts. There is no basis for restricting this to a specific type, rather it includes every addition. The clause ﴿إن الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ (Indeed Allah is over all things competent) is a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, that He ﴿يزيد في الخلق ما يشاء﴾.

﴿ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah grants to mankind, none can withhold it). That is, whatever rain and provision Allah brings them, no one can withhold it, and whatever He withholds from that, no one can release it after He has withheld it. It has also been said: the meaning is that the messengers were sent as a mercy to mankind, so none other than Allah can send them. It has been said: it means supplication. It has been said: it means repentance. It has been said: it means divine success and guidance.

There is no basis for this restriction. Rather the meaning is: whatever Allah opens to mankind from the treasures of His mercy, it includes every blessing with which Allah bestows His creation. Likewise, withholding includes everything Allah withholds from His blessings. He, glory be to Him, is the Giver, the Withholder, the Constrictor and the Expander; there is no giver other than Him and no bestower other than Him.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His servants to remember His blessings, which overflow upon them and which cannot be counted or enumerated: ﴿وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها﴾ (If you counted the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them) [Ibrahim: 34]. The meaning of this command to remember is to guide them to gratitude, to preserve those blessings and to seek more of them.

﴿هل من خالق غير الله﴾ (Is there any creator other than Allah?). Here *min* is redundant (za'ida), *khaliq* is the subject (mubtada'), and *ghayr Allah* is its qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: *ghayr* is in the nominative because the meaning is "Is there a creator other than Allah?", since *min* is an emphasizing redundant particle. Whoever reads *ghayr* in the genitive treats it as a qualifier according to the wording.

The majority of reciters read *ghayr* in the nominative. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive. Al-Fadl ibn Ibrahim read it in the accusative as an exception (istithna'). The clause ﴿يرزقكم من السماء والأرض﴾ (who provides for you from the heaven and the earth) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject, or a resumptive sentence, or another qualifier of *khaliq*, and its predicate is omitted. Provision from the heaven is by rain, and from the earth is by plants and other things. The clause ﴿لا إله إلا هو﴾ (there is no deity but Him) is a resumptive sentence confirming the negation implied by the interrogative. ﴿فأنى تؤفكون﴾ (How then are you deluded?) comes from *al-afk* with a fatha, which means turning away. It is said: "What turned you away from such-and-such?" meaning "What diverted you?" So: "How are you diverted?" It has also been said that it is derived from *al-ifk* with a kasra, meaning lying, because it is turned away from truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, from where does falsehood and denial of the oneness of Allah and of the resurrection come to you, while you acknowledge that Allah created you and provided for you?

Then Allah, glory be to Him, consoled His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, saying: ﴿وإن يكذبوك فقد كذبت رسل من قبلك﴾ (If they deny you, messengers before you were also denied), so that he may take comfort in those prophets who came before him and be consoled regarding the denial of the Meccan disbelievers. ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾ (And to Allah all matters are returned) and not to anyone else, so He will recompense each according to what he deserves.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Ibn Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Watthab, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *turja'* with a fatha on the *ta'* (the second letter), in the active voice. The rest read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

﴿يا أيها الناس إن وعد الله حق﴾ (O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true). That is, His promise of resurrection, gathering, reckoning, punishment, Paradise and Hellfire, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿وإلى الله ترجع الأمور﴾. So let not the life of this world deceive you with its adornment and its pleasures. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the deception of the life of this world is that a person becomes preoccupied with its pleasures and delights instead of the deeds of the Hereafter, until he says: ﴿يا ليتني قدمت لحياتي﴾ (Would that I had sent forth for my life) [al-Fajr: 24]. ﴿ولا يغرنكم بالله الغرور﴾ (Nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah). The majority read *al-ghurur* with a fatha on the *ghayn*, meaning the one who greatly deceives, and this is Satan.

Ibn al-Sikkit and Abu Hatim said: *al-Ghurur* is Satan. It may also be a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj considered this unlikely, because *gharra bihi* is transitive, and the verbal noun of a transitive verb is typically of the form *fa'l*, as in *darabahu darban*, except for a few well-known exceptions that are not used as a basis for analogy. The meaning of the verse is: do not let Satan deceive you about Allah, so that he tells you that Allah will overlook your sins and forgive you because of your merit or because of the vastness of His mercy toward you.

Abu Haywa, Abu al-Simak and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read *al-ghurur* with a damma on the *ghayn*, meaning falsehood.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: *al-ghurur* with a damma is what deceives of the goods of this world.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ghurur* may be the plural of *gharr* (deceiver), like *qa'id* and *qu'ud*. It has been said: it may also be a verbal noun of *gharrahu*, like *al-lizum* and *al-nuhuk*, but against this is what al-Zajjaj said about its unlikelihood.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, warned His servants about Satan, saying: ﴿إن الشيطان لكم عدو فاتخذوه عدوا﴾ (Indeed Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy). That is, oppose him by obeying Allah, and do not obey him in acts of disobedience to Allah.

Then He explained to His servants the manner of Satan's enmity toward them, saying: ﴿إنما يدعو حزبه ليكونوا من أصحاب السعير﴾ (He only invites his party so that they become companions of the Blaze). That is, he only calls his followers, his adherents and those who obey him to acts of disobedience to Allah, glory be to Him, so that they become people of the Fire.

The relative clause in ﴿الذين كفروا لهم عذاب شديد﴾ (Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment) may be in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with ﴿لهم عذاب شديد﴾ as its predicate. It may be in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the subject of *yakunu* (they become). It may be in the accusative as a substitute for *hizbahu*, or as a qualifier of it, or by an implied verb indicating blame. It may be in the genitive as a substitute for *ashab* or as a qualifier of it. The nominative as the subject is the strongest of these possibilities, because after mentioning Satan's enmity and his calling of his party, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the two groups: those who obey him and those who disobey Allah. The first group has a severe punishment, and the other group is described in ﴿والذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات لهم مغفرة وأجر كبير﴾ (But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward). That is, Allah will forgive them because of their faith and righteous deeds, and will give them a great reward, which is Paradise.

﴿أفمن زين له سوء عمله فرآه حسنا﴾ (Is one to whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive so that he sees it as good...?). This sentence is a resumptive sentence confirming the difference previously mentioned between the two groups. *Man* is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted.

Al-Kisa'i said: the implied meaning is "his soul has gone out after them in regrets" (*dhahabat nafsuka 'alayhim hasarat*).

He said: this is indicated by His saying: ﴿فلا تذهب نفسك عليهم حسرات﴾ (So do not let yourself go in regret over them). He said: this is a beautiful Arabic expression that only a few know.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied meaning is "like one whom He guided," and others estimated it as "like one who was not made to see his deed as attractive." This latter is better, because it agrees with the wording and the meaning. The author of *al-Kashshaf* erred: he attributed to al-Zajjaj what al-Kisa'i had said.

Al-Nahhas said: what al-Kisa'i said is the best of what has been said about the verse, because of the indication it gives of the omitted element. The meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, from extreme grief over them and sorrow for them, as He said: ﴿فلعلك باخع نفسك﴾ (Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief) [al-Kahf: 6].

The clause ﴿فإن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي من يشاء﴾ (For indeed Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills) confirms what precedes it, that is: He sends astray whomever He wills to send astray, and guides whomever He wills to guide.
