Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Nor is anyone granted a long life or has a part reduced from his life﴾, the verse, that he said: It says: No one for whom I have decreed a long life and existence, but he will reach what I have decreed for him of lifespan, and I have decreed that for him. He only reaches the Book in which I have determined it, and nothing is added to it. And no one for whom I have decreed that his life is short will reach a longer lifespan, but he reaches the Book which has been written for him. This is His saying: ﴿And none has his life reduced but that it is in a Book﴾, meaning: all of that is in a Book with Him.
Ahmad, Muslim, Abu 'Awanah, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An angel enters upon the drop of semen after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy? Male or female?' Allah decrees, and the two are written. Then he records its deed, its provision, its term, its traces, and its misfortune. Then the scroll is rolled up, and nothing is added to it or reduced from it."
Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Umm Habibah said: 'O Allah, grant me enjoyment of my husband the Prophet, and of my father Abu Sufyan, and of my brother Mu'awiyah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You have asked Allah for fixed terms, numbered days, and apportioned provisions. Allah will not hasten anything before its appointed time, nor delay anything. Had you asked Allah to protect you from the punishment of the Fire, or the punishment of the grave, it would have been better and more excellent.'"
These hadiths are specified by what has been related concerning the acceptance of supplication, and that it struggles with the decree, and by what has been related concerning maintaining family ties, that it increases the lifespan. So there is no contradiction among the evidences, as we have mentioned before.
Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Those you invoke do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, that he said: The qitmir is the peel. In another wording: it is the skin that lies on the back of the pit.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of one kind of His marvelous creation and His great power, so that people would reflect on it and take warning from it. He said: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "al-Riyah" (the winds, plural). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-Rih" (the wind, singular). ﴿So they stir up clouds﴾ uses the present tense after the past tense in order to bring the scene before the mind's eye, because this is more effective in prompting those who take warning to reflect. The meaning of their stirring up the clouds is that they agitate them from where they are. ﴿Then We drive it to a dead land﴾. Abu Ubayda said: its path is that they drive it (fa-tasuquhu), because he said "fa-tuthiru" (they stir up).

It has been said: the point of using the two past tenses after the present tense is to indicate certainty.

Al-Mubarrad said: "mayt" and "mayyit" are the same, and this is the view of the Basrans. He recited:
"He who has died and found rest is not truly dead; the true dead are the dead among the living."

﴿Then We bring the earth to life thereby﴾: that is, We bring the earth to life with rain, by causing to grow what grows in it. Even though rain has not been mentioned previously, the clouds indicate it. Or it means: We bring it to life by means of the clouds, since they are the cause of rain, ﴿after its death﴾, that is, after its dryness. He used "revival" (ihya') metaphorically for the growth of plants and "death" (mawt) for dryness. ﴿Likewise the resurrection﴾: that is, likewise Allah will bring His servants back to life after their death, just as He brought the earth back to life after its death. "Al-Nushur" means the resurrection, from "nasharal-insana nushuran" (he raised the person). The kaf (like) is in the position of the nominative as the predicate: that is, the reviving of the dead is like the reviving of the dead earth. So how can you deny it, when you have witnessed more than once what is like it and similar to it?

﴿Whoever desires honor﴾. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: whoever knows to whom honor belongs, for honor belongs to Allah entirely.

Qatada said: ﴿Whoever desires honor﴾ should seek honor through obedience to Allah. He took the meaning of "then to Allah belongs honor" to be a call to obey the One to whom honor belongs, as one says: "whoever wants wealth, wealth belongs to so-and-so," meaning he should seek it from him.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied sense is: whoever desires honor through the worship of Allah, honor belongs to Him, glory be to Him, for Allah, mighty and majestic, grants him honor in this world and the Hereafter.

It has been said: the intended meaning of ﴿whoever desires honor﴾ is the polytheists, for they sought honor through worshipping idols, as in His saying: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of honor﴾ [Maryam: 81]. It has also been said: the intended meaning is those who sought honor through them (the disbelievers) from among those who professed faith with their tongues, ﴿those who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Do they seek honor with them?﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], and so on. ﴿Then to Allah belongs honor entirely﴾: that is, let him seek it from Him, not from anyone else.

The apparent meaning of the verse is this: whoever desires honor and seeks it, let him seek it from Allah, mighty and majestic, for "to Allah belongs honor entirely", none of it belongs to anyone else. The verse thus includes everyone who seeks honor, and its purpose is to alert people of high station and lofty aspirations to where honor is attained and from which direction it is sought.

﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾: that is, it ascends to Allah and not to anyone else. Its ascent to Him means that He accepts it. Or it means the ascent of the scribes among the angels with what they write in the pages. He singled out "the good word" for mention to show the reward for it, though it encompasses every speech characterized as good: remembrance of Allah, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, recitation of the Qur'an, and other things. So there is no basis for restricting it to the word of monotheism (tawhid), or to praise and glorification.

It has been said: the intended meaning of its ascent is its ascent to the lowest heaven. It has also been said: its ascent means Allah's knowledge of it. As for "and the righteous deed raises it", the meaning is that the righteous deed raises the good word, as al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya and al-Dahhak said. The reasoning is that the good word is not accepted except together with a righteous deed.

It has also been said: the subject of "yarfa'uhu" (raises it) is "the good word," and its object is "the righteous deed." The reasoning is that the righteous deed is not accepted except with monotheism and faith.

It has further been said: the subject of "yarfa'uhu" is a pronoun referring to Allah, mighty and majestic. The meaning is that Allah raises the righteous deed above the good word, because the deed confirms the speech.

It has been said: "and the righteous deed raises its doer", and that is the one who desired honor.

Qatada said: the meaning is that Allah raises the righteous deed for its doer, that is, He accepts it. In this case "and the righteous deed" is the subject of a nominal sentence, whose predicate is "yarfa'uhu"; the same is true according to the view of the one who said "it raises its doer."

The majority read "yas'adu" from the triliteral "sa'ida." "Al-kalimu al-tayyibu" is in the nominative as the subject.

Ali and Ibn Mas'ud read "yus'adu" with a dammah on the present-tense letter, from "as'ada," and "al-kalima al-tayyiba" in the accusative as the object. Al-Dahhak read it in the passive voice. The majority read "al-kalimu," and Abu Abd al-Rahman read "al-kalamu." The majority read "wal-'amalu al-salihu" in the nominative, either by coordination (atf) or as a nominal sentence (ibtida'). Ibn Abi Abla and Isa ibn Umar read it in the accusative under the construction of "ishtighal" (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun).

﴿And those who plot evil deeds, for them there is a severe punishment﴾. The accusative of "al-sayyi'at" (evil deeds) is because it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar): that is, "yamkurruna al-makarati al-sayyi'ati" (they plot evil plottings). This is because "makara" is intransitive, though it may be construed to mean "yaksibuna" (they earn), in which case "al-sayyi'at" is the direct object.

Mujahid and Qatada said: they are the people of showing off (riya').

Abu al-Aliya said: they are those who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh).

Al-Kalbi said: they are those who commit evil deeds in this world.

Muqatil said: they are the polytheists. The meaning of ﴿for them there is a severe punishment﴾ is: for them there is a punishment reaching the utmost extreme of severity. ﴿And the plotting of those will come to nothing﴾: that is, it will be nullified and perish. From the same root is ﴿and you were a people who perished﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. "Makr" (plotting) originally means deception and cunning. The reference of "ula'ika" (those) is to those who plotted evil deeds, according to the differing views on the interpretation of their plotting. The clause ﴿it will perish﴾ is the predicate of "makru ula'ika" (the plotting of those).

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another proof of the resurrection and return, saying: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾: that is, He created you at the beginning within the creation of your father Adam from dust.

Qatada said: it means Adam. The implied meaning according to this is: He created your first father, the origin to which you return, from dust. ﴿Then from a drop of semen (nutfah) which He brought forth from the loins of your fathers﴾. ﴿Then He made you pairs﴾: that is, He paired some of you with others, so the male is a mate to the female. Or it means He made you kinds, males and females. ﴿And no female conceives or bears except with His knowledge﴾: that is, no conception or birth occurs except that Allah knows it, so nothing escapes His knowledge and governance. ﴿And no one is granted length of life, nor is any of his life shortened, except it is in a Book﴾: that is, no one's life is lengthened, and no one's life is shortened, except that it is in a Book, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Al-Farra' said: He means another, not the first, so He referred to it with a pronoun as though it were the first, because if the second noun were stated explicitly it would be like the first. It is as though He said: "nor is any of the life of one granted length shortened." So the pronoun in "his life" refers to another, not the first, just as your saying "I have a dirham and its half", meaning another half.

It has been said: he was called "one granted length of life" only in view of his eventual end.

The meaning is: no one's life is extended, and no one's life is shortened, but not in the sense that it is shortened after having been extended; rather, it means that no one's life is made short from the beginning except that it is in a Book.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿And no one is granted length of life﴾ except that his life is written: how many years, how many months, how many days, how many hours. Then it is written in another book: an hour has been cut from his life, a day has been cut from his life, a month has been cut, a year has been cut, until he fulfills his term. Thus what has passed of his term is the shortening, and what is still to come is what is granted.

Qatada said: the one granted length of life is the one who reaches sixty years, and the one whose life is shortened is the one who dies before sixty years.

It has been said: the meaning is that Allah wrote a person's life as such-and-such if he obeys, and recorded it differently if he disobeys. Whichever of these he reaches, it is in the Book. The pronoun in this view refers to "one granted length of life."

It has been said: the meaning is: no one is granted length of life up to old age, and no one else has his life shortened from old age, except that it is in a Book, that is, by the decree of Allah. This was said by al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

He (al-Nahhas) said: it is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of the revelation. The better view is to say: the apparent sense of the Qur'anic text is that the lengthening and shortening of life are both by the decree and destiny of Allah, for reasons that require lengthening and reasons that require shortening.

Among the causes of lengthening is what has been reported concerning maintaining family ties (silat al-rahim) from the Prophet (ﷺ) and similar matters.

Among the causes of shortening is excessive disobedience to Allah, mighty and majestic. So if the lifespan decreed for a man is, for example, seventy years, Allah may add to it if he does the causes of increase, and He may reduce it if he does the causes of decrease. All of it is in a Clear Book. There is therefore no contradiction between this verse and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. This is supported by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39]. We have already presented in our commentary on it what makes what we have mentioned here clearer and more explicit.

The majority read "yunqasu" in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Sallam, and what is reported from Abu Amr read "yanqusu" in the active voice.

The majority read "min 'umurihi" with a dammah on the mim. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read it with a sukun on it.

The reference of "inna dhalika" (indeed that) is to what preceded of the creation and what follows: ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, not difficult for Him in any respect, and nothing escapes Him, whether much or little, great or small.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous creation and wondrous power, saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter﴾. So "the two seas" refers to the sweet and the salty. "Al-'adhb" is sweet, and "al-furat" is very sweet, while "al-ujaj" is bitter. "Sa'igh sharabuhu" means that its drink goes down the throat easily because of its sweetness.

Isa ibn Umar read "sayygh" with a shaddah on the ya'. It is also reported that he read it with a sukun.

Talha and Abu Nahik read "milh" with a fathah on the mim. ﴿And from both you eat fresh flesh﴾: this refers to what is caught from both of them, of their animals that are eaten. ﴿And you extract ornaments which you wear﴾. The apparent meaning is: and you extract from them ornaments which you wear.

Al-Mubarrad said: ornaments are extracted only from the salty water. It is reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: ornaments are extracted from both when they mix, not from each one separately. Al-Nahhas preferred the view of al-Mubarrad.

The meaning of "which you wear" is that you wear each thing of them according to its kind, such as a ring on the finger, a bracelet on the arm, a necklace on the neck, an anklet on the leg. Among what is worn is the ornamentation of weapons that are carried, such as the sword, the coat of mail, and the like.

﴿And you see the ships in it﴾: that is, in each of the two seas. Al-Nahhas said: the pronoun refers only to the salty water, for otherwise it would have said "in them" (fihima) and "plowing" (mawakhir). "Makhara al-safinatu yamkhuru" means the ship plowed the water when it cut through it.

So the meaning is: you see the ships in the two seas cutting through the water, some coming and some going, by one wind. The discussion of this has already been presented in Surat al-Nahl. The lam in ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is related to what the preceding speech indicates: that is, He did this so that you might seek, or it is related to "mawakhir" (plowing).

Mujahid said: seeking the bounty is trade by sea to distant lands in a short time, as has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿And perhaps you will give thanks﴾ to Allah for the blessings He has bestowed upon you through that.

Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of the verse is to provide a parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, and between disbelief and faith. Just as the two seas are not alike, so the believer and the disbeliever are not alike, nor are disbelief and faith alike.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, i.e., He adds some parts of each of them to the other, so that one increases by the decrease of the other. Its explanation has already been given in Al 'Imran (Al 'Imran), and in other places of the Noble Book. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾, which Allah determined for their courses, and it is the Day of Resurrection.
It was said: it is the period in which they traverse the orbit, which is a year for the sun and a month for the moon.
It was said: what is meant is the course of the sun in a day and of the moon in a night.
The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Luqman. The reference in His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ is to the doer of these actions, who is Allah, glorified is He. The demonstrative noun is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Allah, your Lord, to Him belongs the dominion﴾, i.e., this One who is the maker of what has preceded is the Creator who determines, the Capable who has power, the Owner of the world, and the One who disposes of it. It is also permissible that His saying "to Him belongs the dominion" be an independent sentence in contrast to His saying ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, i.e., they have no power over it or over its creation. The qitmir is the thin skin that lies between the date and the pit, and which clings to the pit like a wrapping around it. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the split of the pit. Qatadah said: it is the cup-like cavity on the top of the pit. Al-Jawhari said: it is said to be the white speck on the back of the pit from which the palm tree sprouts.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear the state of those whom they invoke besides Allah, that they neither benefit nor harm, so He said: ﴿If you invoke them, they will not hear your call﴾, i.e., if you seek their help in calamities, they will not hear your call, because they are inanimate objects that perceive nothing of what is perceptible. ﴿And if they could hear﴾, by way of supposition and assumption, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, because of their inability in that regard.
Qatadah said: the meaning is, even if they heard, they would not benefit you.
It was said: the meaning is: if We had given them hearing and life so that they heard your call, they would have been more obedient to Allah than you, and they would not have responded to you regarding what you invoked them to, namely disbelief. On the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association [of them with Allah], i.e., they will disown your worship of them, and they will say: ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 28]. It is also permissible that ﴿Those you invoke besides Him﴾ [Al-A'raf: 197] and what follows it refer to those who have intellect among those whom the disbelievers worshipped, and they are the angels, the jinn, and the devils.
The meaning is: they deny that what you did was true, and they deny that they had commanded you to worship them. ﴿And none can inform you like one who is Acquainted﴾, i.e., none informs you like one who is All-Knowing of things and aware of them, and that is Allah, glorified is He, for there is no one more informed about His creation, their statements and their actions than He, glorified is He, and He is the Acquainted with the reality and true nature of affairs.
Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: An angel will stand with the Trumpet between the heaven and the earth, and he will blow into it, and no creature of Allah in the heavens and the earth will remain, except whom Allah wills, but will die. Then Allah will send down from beneath the Throne a semen like the semen of men, and their bodies and flesh will grow from that water as the earth grows from the moist soil. Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾, the verse.
Abu Dawud, al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah give life to the dead?" He said: "Have you not passed by a barren land and then passed by it fertile, stirring green?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and thus is the resurrection."
'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When we narrate to you a hadith, we bring you confirmation of it from the Book of Allah: indeed, when the Muslim servant says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and "All praise is for Allah," and "There is no god but Allah," and "Allah is greatest," and "Blessed is Allah," a angel takes hold of them, gathers them under his wing, and then ascends with them to the heaven. He does not pass with them by a company of angels except that they seek forgiveness for the one who said them, until he brings them to the Face of the Most Merciful. Then he recited: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾, and said: "It is the performance of the obligatory duties. Whoever mentions Allah while performing his obligatory duties, his deed carries the remembrance of Allah, and it ascends with it to Allah. But whoever mentions Allah and does not perform his obligatory duties, his words are returned upon his deed, and his deed is more deserving of it."
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Nor is anyone granted a long life or has a part reduced from his life﴾, the verse, that he said: It says: No one for whom I have decreed a long life and existence, but he will reach what I have decreed for him of lifespan, and I have decreed that for him. He only reaches the Book in which I have determined it, and nothing is added to it. And no one for whom I have decreed that his life is short will reach a longer lifespan, but he reaches the Book which has been written for him. This is His saying: ﴿And none has his life reduced but that it is in a Book﴾, meaning: all of that is in a Book with Him.
Ahmad, Muslim, Abu 'Awanah, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An angel enters upon the drop of semen after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy? Male or female?' Allah decrees, and the two are written. Then he records its deed, its provision, its term, its traces, and its misfortune. Then the scroll is rolled up, and nothing is added to it or reduced from it."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You have asked Allah for fixed terms, numbered days, and apportioned provisions. Allah will not hasten anything before its appointed time, nor delay anything. Had you asked Allah to protect you from the punishment of the Fire, or the punishment of the grave, it would have been better and more excellent.'"

So there is no contradiction among the evidences, as we have mentioned before.

"He who has died and found rest is not truly dead; the true dead are the dead among the living."

﴿Then We bring the earth to life thereby﴾: that is, We bring the earth to life with rain, by causing to grow what grows in it. Even though rain has not been mentioned previously, the clouds indicate it. Or it means: We bring it to life by means of the clouds, since they are the cause of rain, ﴿after its death﴾, that is, after its dryness. It has also been said: the intended meaning is those who sought honor through them (the disbelievers) from among those who professed faith with their tongues, ﴿those who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Do they seek honor with them?﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], and so on. ﴿Then to Allah belongs honor entirely﴾: that is, let him seek it from Him, not from anyone else.

﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾: that is, it ascends to Allah and not to anyone else. Its ascent to Him means that He accepts it. Or it means the ascent of the scribes among the angels with what they write in the pages. He singled out "the good word" for mention to show the reward for it, though it encompasses every speech characterized as good: remembrance of Allah, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, recitation of the Qur'an, and other things. So there is no basis for restricting it to the word of monotheism (tawhid), or to praise and glorification.

It has been said: the intended meaning of its ascent is its ascent to the lowest heaven. It has also been said: its ascent means Allah's knowledge of it. As for "and the righteous deed raises it", the meaning is that the righteous deed raises the good word, as al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya and al-Dahhak said. The reasoning is that the good word is not accepted except together with a righteous deed.

It has also been said: the subject of "yarfa'uhu" (raises it) is "the good word," and its object is "the righteous deed." The reasoning is that the righteous deed is not accepted except with monotheism and faith.

It has further been said: the subject of "yarfa'uhu" is a pronoun referring to Allah, mighty and majestic. The meaning is that Allah raises the righteous deed above the good word, because the deed confirms the speech.

It has been said: "and the righteous deed raises its doer", and that is the one who desired honor.

Qatada said: the meaning is that Allah raises the righteous deed for its doer, that is, He accepts it. In this case "and the righteous deed" is the subject of a nominal sentence, whose predicate is "yarfa'uhu"; the same is true according to the view of the one who said "it raises its doer."

The majority read "yas'adu" from the triliteral "sa'ida." "Al-kalimu al-tayyibu" is in the nominative as the subject.

Ali and Ibn Mas'ud read "yus'adu" with a dammah on the present-tense letter, from "as'ada," and "al-kalima al-tayyiba" in the accusative as the object. Al-Dahhak read it in the passive voice. The majority read "al-kalimu," and Abu Abd al-Rahman read "al-kalamu." The majority read "wal-'amalu al-salihu" in the nominative, either by coordination (atf) or as a nominal sentence (ibtida'). Ibn Abi Abla and Isa ibn Umar read it in the accusative under the construction of "ishtighal" (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun).

﴿And those who plot evil deeds, for them there is a severe punishment﴾. The accusative of "al-sayyi'at" (evil deeds) is because it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar): that is, "yamkurruna al-makarati al-sayyi'ati" (they plot evil plottings). This is because "makara" is intransitive, though it may be construed to mean "yaksibuna" (they earn), in which case "al-sayyi'at" is the direct object.

Mujahid and Qatada said: they are the people of showing off (riya').

Abu al-Aliya said: they are those who plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) when they gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh).

Al-Kalbi said: they are those who commit evil deeds in this world.

Muqatil said: they are the polytheists. The meaning of ﴿for them there is a severe punishment﴾ is: for them there is a punishment reaching the utmost extreme of severity. ﴿And the plotting of those will come to nothing﴾: that is, it will be nullified and perish. From the same root is ﴿and you were a people who perished﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. "Makr" (plotting) originally means deception and cunning. The reference of "ula'ika" (those) is to those who plotted evil deeds, according to the differing views on the interpretation of their plotting. The clause ﴿it will perish﴾ is the predicate of "makru ula'ika" (the plotting of those).

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another proof of the resurrection and return, saying: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾: that is, He created you at the beginning within the creation of your father Adam from dust.

Qatada said: it means Adam. The implied meaning according to this is: He created your first father, the origin to which you return, from dust. ﴿Then from a drop of semen (nutfah) which He brought forth from the loins of your fathers﴾. ﴿Then He made you pairs﴾: that is, He paired some of you with others, so the male is a mate to the female. Or it means He made you kinds, males and females. ﴿And no female conceives or bears except with His knowledge﴾: that is, no conception or birth occurs except that Allah knows it, so nothing escapes His knowledge and governance. ﴿And no one is granted length of life, nor is any of his life shortened, except it is in a Book﴾: that is, no one's life is lengthened, and no one's life is shortened, except that it is in a Book, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Al-Farra' said: He means another, not the first, so He referred to it with a pronoun as though it were the first, because if the second noun were stated explicitly it would be like the first. It is as though He said: "nor is any of the life of one granted length shortened." So the pronoun in "his life" refers to another, not the first, just as your saying "I have a dirham and its half", meaning another half.

It has been said: he was called "one granted length of life" only in view of his eventual end.

The meaning is: no one's life is extended, and no one's life is shortened, but not in the sense that it is shortened after having been extended; rather, it means that no one's life is made short from the beginning except that it is in a Book.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿And no one is granted length of life﴾ except that his life is written: how many years, how many months, how many days, how many hours. Then it is written in another book: an hour has been cut from his life, a day has been cut from his life, a month has been cut, a year has been cut, until he fulfills his term. Thus what has passed of his term is the shortening, and what is still to come is what is granted.

Qatada said: the one granted length of life is the one who reaches sixty years, and the one whose life is shortened is the one who dies before sixty years.

It has been said: the meaning is that Allah wrote a person's life as such-and-such if he obeys, and recorded it differently if he disobeys. Whichever of these he reaches, it is in the Book. The pronoun in this view refers to "one granted length of life."

It has been said: the meaning is: no one is granted length of life up to old age, and no one else has his life shortened from old age, except that it is in a Book, that is, by the decree of Allah. This was said by al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

He (al-Nahhas) said: it is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of the revelation. The better view is to say: the apparent sense of the Qur'anic text is that the lengthening and shortening of life are both by the decree and destiny of Allah, for reasons that require lengthening and reasons that require shortening.

Among the causes of lengthening is what has been reported concerning maintaining family ties (silat al-rahim) from the Prophet (ﷺ) and similar matters.

Among the causes of shortening is excessive disobedience to Allah, mighty and majestic. So if the lifespan decreed for a man is, for example, seventy years, Allah may add to it if he does the causes of increase, and He may reduce it if he does the causes of decrease. All of it is in a Clear Book. There is therefore no contradiction between this verse and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. This is supported by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39]. We have already presented in our commentary on it what makes what we have mentioned here clearer and more explicit.

The majority read "yunqasu" in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Sallam, and what is reported from Abu Amr read "yanqusu" in the active voice.

The majority read "min 'umurihi" with a dammah on the mim. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read it with a sukun on it.

The reference of "inna dhalika" (indeed that) is to what preceded of the creation and what follows: ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, not difficult for Him in any respect, and nothing escapes Him, whether much or little, great or small.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous creation and wondrous power, saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter﴾. So "the two seas" refers to the sweet and the salty. "Al-'adhb" is sweet, and "al-furat" is very sweet, while "al-ujaj" is bitter. "Sa'igh sharabuhu" means that its drink goes down the throat easily because of its sweetness.

Isa ibn Umar read "sayygh" with a shaddah on the ya'. It is also reported that he read it with a sukun.

Talha and Abu Nahik read "milh" with a fathah on the mim. ﴿And from both you eat fresh flesh﴾: this refers to what is caught from both of them, of their animals that are eaten. ﴿And you extract ornaments which you wear﴾. The apparent meaning is: and you extract from them ornaments which you wear.

Al-Mubarrad said: ornaments are extracted only from the salty water. It is reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: ornaments are extracted from both when they mix, not from each one separately. Al-Nahhas preferred the view of al-Mubarrad.

The meaning of "which you wear" is that you wear each thing of them according to its kind, such as a ring on the finger, a bracelet on the arm, a necklace on the neck, an anklet on the leg. Among what is worn is the ornamentation of weapons that are carried, such as the sword, the coat of mail, and the like.

﴿And you see the ships in it﴾: that is, in each of the two seas. Al-Nahhas said: the pronoun refers only to the salty water, for otherwise it would have said "in them" (fihima) and "plowing" (mawakhir). "Makhara al-safinatu yamkhuru" means the ship plowed the water when it cut through it.

So the meaning is: you see the ships in the two seas cutting through the water, some coming and some going, by one wind. The discussion of this has already been presented in Surat al-Nahl. The lam in ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is related to what the preceding speech indicates: that is, He did this so that you might seek, or it is related to "mawakhir" (plowing).

Mujahid said: seeking the bounty is trade by sea to distant lands in a short time, as has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿And perhaps you will give thanks﴾ to Allah for the blessings He has bestowed upon you through that.

Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of the verse is to provide a parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, and between disbelief and faith. Just as the two seas are not alike, so the believer and the disbeliever are not alike, nor are disbelief and faith alike.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, i.e., He adds some parts of each of them to the other, so that one increases by the decrease of the other. Its explanation has already been given in Al 'Imran (Al 'Imran), and in other places of the Noble Book. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾, which Allah determined for their courses, and it is the Day of Resurrection.
It was said: it is the period in which they traverse the orbit, which is a year for the sun and a month for the moon.
It was said: what is meant is the course of the sun in a day and of the moon in a night.
The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Luqman. The reference in His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ is to the doer of these actions, who is Allah, glorified is He. The demonstrative noun is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Allah, your Lord, to Him belongs the dominion﴾, i.e., this One who is the maker of what has preceded is the Creator who determines, the Capable who has power, the Owner of the world, and the One who disposes of it. It is also permissible that His saying "to Him belongs the dominion" be an independent sentence in contrast to His saying ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, i.e., they have no power over it or over its creation. The qitmir is the thin skin that lies between the date and the pit, and which clings to the pit like a wrapping around it. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the split of the pit. Qatadah said: it is the cup-like cavity on the top of the pit. Al-Jawhari said: it is said to be the white speck on the back of the pit from which the palm tree sprouts.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear the state of those whom they invoke besides Allah, that they neither benefit nor harm, so He said: ﴿If you invoke them, they will not hear your call﴾, i.e., if you seek their help in calamities, they will not hear your call, because they are inanimate objects that perceive nothing of what is perceptible. ﴿And if they could hear﴾, by way of supposition and assumption, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, because of their inability in that regard.
Qatadah said: the meaning is, even if they heard, they would not benefit you.
It was said: the meaning is: if We had given them hearing and life so that they heard your call, they would have been more obedient to Allah than you, and they would not have responded to you regarding what you invoked them to, namely disbelief. On the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association [of them with Allah], i.e., they will disown your worship of them, and they will say: ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 28]. It is also permissible that ﴿Those you invoke besides Him﴾ [Al-A'raf: 197] and what follows it refer to those who have intellect among those whom the disbelievers worshipped, and they are the angels, the jinn, and the devils.
The meaning is: they deny that what you did was true, and they deny that they had commanded you to worship them. ﴿And none can inform you like one who is Acquainted﴾, i.e., none informs you like one who is All-Knowing of things and aware of them, and that is Allah, glorified is He, for there is no one more informed about His creation, their statements and their actions than He, glorified is He, and He is the Acquainted with the reality and true nature of affairs.
Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: An angel will stand with the Trumpet between the heaven and the earth, and he will blow into it, and no creature of Allah in the heavens and the earth will remain, except whom Allah wills, but will die. Then Allah will send down from beneath the Throne a semen like the semen of men, and their bodies and flesh will grow from that water as the earth grows from the moist soil. Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾, the verse.
Abu Dawud, al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah give life to the dead?" He said: "Have you not passed by a barren land and then passed by it fertile, stirring green?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and thus is the resurrection."
'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When we narrate to you a hadith, we bring you confirmation of it from the Book of Allah: indeed, when the Muslim servant says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and "All praise is for Allah," and "There is no god but Allah," and "Allah is greatest," and "Blessed is Allah," a angel takes hold of them, gathers them under his wing, and then ascends with them to the heaven. He does not pass with them by a company of angels except that they seek forgiveness for the one who said them, until he brings them to the Face of the Most Merciful. Then he recited: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾, and said: "It is the performance of the obligatory duties. Whoever mentions Allah while performing his obligatory duties, his deed carries the remembrance of Allah, and it ascends with it to Allah. But whoever mentions Allah and does not perform his obligatory duties, his words are returned upon his deed, and his deed is more deserving of it."
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Nor is anyone granted a long life or has a part reduced from his life﴾, the verse, that he said: It says: No one for whom I have decreed a long life and existence, but he will reach what I have decreed for him of lifespan, and I have decreed that for him. He only reaches the Book in which I have determined it, and nothing is added to it. And no one for whom I have decreed that his life is short will reach a longer lifespan, but he reaches the Book which has been written for him. This is His saying: ﴿And none has his life reduced but that it is in a Book﴾, meaning: all of that is in a Book with Him.
Ahmad, Muslim, Abu 'Awanah, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An angel enters upon the drop of semen after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy? Male or female?' Allah decrees, and the two are written. Then he records its deed, its provision, its term, its traces, and its misfortune. Then the scroll is rolled up, and nothing is added to it or reduced from it."
Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Umm Habibah said: 'O Allah, grant me enjoyment of my husband the Prophet, and of my father Abu Sufyan, and of my brother Mu'awiyah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You have asked Allah for fixed terms, numbered days, and apportioned provisions. Allah will not hasten anything before its appointed time, nor delay anything. Had you asked Allah to protect you from the punishment of the Fire, or the punishment of the grave, it would have been better and more excellent.'"
These hadiths are specified by what has been related concerning the acceptance of supplication, and that it struggles with the decree, and by what has been related concerning maintaining family ties, that it increases the lifespan. So there is no contradiction among the evidences, as we have mentioned before.
Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Those you invoke do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, that he said: The qitmir is the peel. In another wording: it is the skin that lies on the back of the pit.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of one kind of His marvelous creation and His great power, so that people would reflect on it and take warning from it. He said: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "al-Riyah" (the winds, plural). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-Rih" (the wind, singular). ﴿So they stir up clouds﴾ uses the present tense after the past tense in order to bring the scene before the mind's eye, because this is more effective in prompting those who take warning to reflect. The meaning of their stirring up the clouds is that they agitate them from where they are. ﴿Then We drive it to a dead land﴾. Abu Ubayda said: its path is that they drive it (fa-tasuquhu), because he said "fa-tuthiru" (they stir up).

It has been said: the point of using the two past tenses after the present tense is to indicate certainty.

Al-Mubarrad said: "mayt" and "mayyit" are the same, and this is the view of the Basrans. He recited:
"He who has died and found rest is not truly dead; the true dead are the dead among the living."

﴿Then We bring the earth to life thereby﴾: that is, We bring the earth to life with rain, by causing to grow what grows in it. Even though rain has not been mentioned previously, the clouds indicate it. Or it means: We bring it to life by means of the clouds, since they are the cause of rain, ﴿after its death﴾, that is, after its dryness. He used "revival" (ihya') metaphorically for the growth of plants and "death" (mawt) for dryness. ﴿Likewise the resurrection﴾: that is, likewise Allah will bring His servants back to life after their death, just as He brought the earth back to life after its death. "Al-Nushur" means the resurrection, from "nasharal-insana nushuran" (he raised the person). The kaf (like) is in the position of the nominative as the predicate: that is, the reviving of the dead is like the reviving of the dead earth. So how can you deny it, when you have witnessed more than once what is like it and similar to it?

Qatada said: ﴿Whoever desires honor﴾ should seek honor through obedience to Allah. He took the meaning of "then to Allah belongs honor" to be a call to obey the One to whom honor belongs, as one says: "whoever wants wealth, wealth belongs to so-and-so," meaning he should seek it from him.

Al-Zajjaj said: its implied sense is: whoever desires honor through the worship of Allah, honor belongs to Him, glory be to Him, for Allah, mighty and majestic, grants him honor in this world and the Hereafter.

It has been said: the intended meaning of ﴿whoever desires honor﴾ is the polytheists, for they sought honor through worshipping idols, as in His saying: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of honor﴾ [Maryam: 81]. It has also been said: the intended meaning is those who sought honor through them (the disbelievers) from among those who professed faith with their tongues, ﴿those who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers. Do they seek honor with them?﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], and so on. ﴿Then to Allah belongs honor entirely﴾: that is, let him seek it from Him, not from anyone else.

The apparent meaning of the verse is this: whoever desires honor and seeks it, let him seek it from Allah, mighty and majestic, for "to Allah belongs honor entirely", none of it belongs to anyone else. The verse thus includes everyone who seeks honor, and its purpose is to alert people of high station and lofty aspirations to where honor is attained and from which direction it is sought.

Qatada said: the one granted length of life is the one who reaches sixty years, and the one whose life is shortened is the one who dies before sixty years.

It has been said: the meaning is that Allah wrote a person's life as such-and-such if he obeys, and recorded it differently if he disobeys. Whichever of these he reaches, it is in the Book. The pronoun in this view refers to "one granted length of life."

It has been said: the meaning is: no one is granted length of life up to old age, and no one else has his life shortened from old age, except that it is in a Book, that is, by the decree of Allah. This was said by al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

He (al-Nahhas) said: it is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of the revelation. The better view is to say: the apparent sense of the Qur'anic text is that the lengthening and shortening of life are both by the decree and destiny of Allah, for reasons that require lengthening and reasons that require shortening.

Among the causes of lengthening is what has been reported concerning maintaining family ties (silat al-rahim) from the Prophet (ﷺ) and similar matters.

Among the causes of shortening is excessive disobedience to Allah, mighty and majestic. So if the lifespan decreed for a man is, for example, seventy years, Allah may add to it if he does the causes of increase, and He may reduce it if he does the causes of decrease. All of it is in a Clear Book. There is therefore no contradiction between this verse and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. This is supported by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39]. We have already presented in our commentary on it what makes what we have mentioned here clearer and more explicit.

The majority read "yunqasu" in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Sallam, and what is reported from Abu Amr read "yanqusu" in the active voice.

The majority read "min 'umurihi" with a dammah on the mim. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read it with a sukun on it.

The reference of "inna dhalika" (indeed that) is to what preceded of the creation and what follows: ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, not difficult for Him in any respect, and nothing escapes Him, whether much or little, great or small.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous creation and wondrous power, saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter﴾. So "the two seas" refers to the sweet and the salty. "Al-'adhb" is sweet, and "al-furat" is very sweet, while "al-ujaj" is bitter. "Sa'igh sharabuhu" means that its drink goes down the throat easily because of its sweetness.

Isa ibn Umar read "sayygh" with a shaddah on the ya'. It is also reported that he read it with a sukun.

Talha and Abu Nahik read "milh" with a fathah on the mim. ﴿And from both you eat fresh flesh﴾: this refers to what is caught from both of them, of their animals that are eaten. ﴿And you extract ornaments which you wear﴾. The apparent meaning is: and you extract from them ornaments which you wear.

Al-Mubarrad said: ornaments are extracted only from the salty water. It is reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: ornaments are extracted from both when they mix, not from each one separately. Al-Nahhas preferred the view of al-Mubarrad.

The meaning of "which you wear" is that you wear each thing of them according to its kind, such as a ring on the finger, a bracelet on the arm, a necklace on the neck, an anklet on the leg. Among what is worn is the ornamentation of weapons that are carried, such as the sword, the coat of mail, and the like.

﴿And you see the ships in it﴾: that is, in each of the two seas. Al-Nahhas said: the pronoun refers only to the salty water, for otherwise it would have said "in them" (fihima) and "plowing" (mawakhir). "Makhara al-safinatu yamkhuru" means the ship plowed the water when it cut through it.

So the meaning is: you see the ships in the two seas cutting through the water, some coming and some going, by one wind. The discussion of this has already been presented in Surat al-Nahl. The lam in ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is related to what the preceding speech indicates: that is, He did this so that you might seek, or it is related to "mawakhir" (plowing).

Mujahid said: seeking the bounty is trade by sea to distant lands in a short time, as has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿And perhaps you will give thanks﴾ to Allah for the blessings He has bestowed upon you through that.

Most of the exegetes said: the intended meaning of the verse is to provide a parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, and between disbelief and faith. Just as the two seas are not alike, so the believer and the disbeliever are not alike, nor are disbelief and faith alike.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, i.e., He adds some parts of each of them to the other, so that one increases by the decrease of the other. Its explanation has already been given in Al 'Imran (Al 'Imran), and in other places of the Noble Book. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾, which Allah determined for their courses, and it is the Day of Resurrection.
It was said: it is the period in which they traverse the orbit, which is a year for the sun and a month for the moon.
It was said: what is meant is the course of the sun in a day and of the moon in a night.
The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Luqman. The reference in His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ is to the doer of these actions, who is Allah, glorified is He. The demonstrative noun is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿Allah, your Lord, to Him belongs the dominion﴾, i.e., this One who is the maker of what has preceded is the Creator who determines, the Capable who has power, the Owner of the world, and the One who disposes of it. It is also permissible that His saying "to Him belongs the dominion" be an independent sentence in contrast to His saying ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, i.e., they have no power over it or over its creation. The qitmir is the thin skin that lies between the date and the pit, and which clings to the pit like a wrapping around it. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the split of the pit. Qatadah said: it is the cup-like cavity on the top of the pit. Al-Jawhari said: it is said to be the white speck on the back of the pit from which the palm tree sprouts.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear the state of those whom they invoke besides Allah, that they neither benefit nor harm, so He said: ﴿If you invoke them, they will not hear your call﴾, i.e., if you seek their help in calamities, they will not hear your call, because they are inanimate objects that perceive nothing of what is perceptible. ﴿And if they could hear﴾, by way of supposition and assumption, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, because of their inability in that regard.
Qatadah said: the meaning is, even if they heard, they would not benefit you.
It was said: the meaning is: if We had given them hearing and life so that they heard your call, they would have been more obedient to Allah than you, and they would not have responded to you regarding what you invoked them to, namely disbelief. On the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association [of them with Allah], i.e., they will disown your worship of them, and they will say: ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 28]. It is also permissible that ﴿Those you invoke besides Him﴾ [Al-A'raf: 197] and what follows it refer to those who have intellect among those whom the disbelievers worshipped, and they are the angels, the jinn, and the devils.
The meaning is: they deny that what you did was true, and they deny that they had commanded you to worship them. ﴿And none can inform you like one who is Acquainted﴾, i.e., none informs you like one who is All-Knowing of things and aware of them, and that is Allah, glorified is He, for there is no one more informed about His creation, their statements and their actions than He, glorified is He, and He is the Acquainted with the reality and true nature of affairs.
Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: An angel will stand with the Trumpet between the heaven and the earth, and he will blow into it, and no creature of Allah in the heavens and the earth will remain, except whom Allah wills, but will die. Then Allah will send down from beneath the Throne a semen like the semen of men, and their bodies and flesh will grow from that water as the earth grows from the moist soil. Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾, the verse.
Abu Dawud, al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah give life to the dead?" He said: "Have you not passed by a barren land and then passed by it fertile, stirring green?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and thus is the resurrection."
'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When we narrate to you a hadith, we bring you confirmation of it from the Book of Allah: indeed, when the Muslim servant says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and "All praise is for Allah," and "There is no god but Allah," and "Allah is greatest," and "Blessed is Allah," a angel takes hold of them, gathers them under his wing, and then ascends with them to the heaven. He does not pass with them by a company of angels except that they seek forgiveness for the one who said them, until he brings them to the Face of the Most Merciful. Then he recited: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾, and said: "It is the performance of the obligatory duties. Whoever mentions Allah while performing his obligatory duties, his deed carries the remembrance of Allah, and it ascends with it to Allah. But whoever mentions Allah and does not perform his obligatory duties, his words are returned upon his deed, and his deed is more deserving of it."
Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Nor is anyone granted a long life or has a part reduced from his life﴾, the verse, that he said: It says: No one for whom I have decreed a long life and existence, but he will reach what I have decreed for him of lifespan, and I have decreed that for him. He only reaches the Book in which I have determined it, and nothing is added to it. And no one for whom I have decreed that his life is short will reach a longer lifespan, but he reaches the Book which has been written for him. This is His saying: ﴿And none has his life reduced but that it is in a Book﴾, meaning: all of that is in a Book with Him.
Ahmad, Muslim, Abu 'Awanah, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An angel enters upon the drop of semen after it has settled in the womb for forty or forty-five nights, and says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy? Male or female?' Allah decrees, and the two are written. Then he records its deed, its provision, its term, its traces, and its misfortune. Then the scroll is rolled up, and nothing is added to it or reduced from it."
Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Umm Habibah said: 'O Allah, grant me enjoyment of my husband the Prophet, and of my father Abu Sufyan, and of my brother Mu'awiyah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'You have asked Allah for fixed terms, numbered days, and apportioned provisions. Allah will not hasten anything before its appointed time, nor delay anything. Had you asked Allah to protect you from the punishment of the Fire, or the punishment of the grave, it would have been better and more excellent.'"
These hadiths are specified by what has been related concerning the acceptance of supplication, and that it struggles with the decree, and by what has been related concerning maintaining family ties, that it increases the lifespan. So there is no contradiction among the evidences, as we have mentioned before.
Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Those you invoke do not possess [even] a thin membrane of a date seed﴾, that he said: The qitmir is the peel. In another wording: it is the skin that lies on the back of the pit.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the neediness of His creatures toward Him and their great need for His bounty, and said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward God﴾, that is, those in need of Him in all matters of the religion and the world, so they are poor toward Him absolutely. ﴿And God is the Rich﴾, absolutely, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the one deserving praise from His servants for His kindness toward them.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned one of the ways in which their neediness toward Him and His independence of them is made manifest, saying: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation﴾, that is, if He wills, He will annihilate you and bring in your place a new creation that obeys Him and does not disobey Him, or He will bring a kind of created beings and a world other than what you know.

﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾, that is, it is not impossible or hard for Him. The explanation of this has already passed in Surat Ibrahim.

﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾, that is, no bearing soul, so the qualified noun (mawsuf) was omitted because it is known. The meaning of tazir is "bears" (tahmil).

The meaning: no soul bears the load of another soul, that is, its sin; rather, every soul bears its own burden. This verse does not contradict His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-Ankabut: 13], because they only bore the burdens of their misguiding others along with the burdens of their own misguidance, and all of it is from their own burdens, not from the burdens of others. A similar example is the hadith: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection," for the one who established the evil practice bears only the burden of his own evil practice. The discussion of this verse has already been given in full.

﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load﴾. Al-Farra' said: that is, a heavily laden soul. He said: this applies to both the masculine and the feminine.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, ﴿and if one heavily laden calls﴾ a person to its load, which is its sins, ﴿nothing of it will be carried﴾, that is, none of its load will be borne, ﴿even if he were a close relative﴾, that is, even if the one it calls were a relative of it, he would not bear any of its load.

The meaning of the verse: if a soul burdened with sins calls another soul to bear some of its sins along with it, that summoned soul will not bear any of those sins, even if it were a close relative by lineage. How then with others who have no kinship between them and the one who calls them?

It was read as "dhu qurba" (a close relative), with kana (was) taken as a complete verb, like His saying: ﴿And if there is one in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280].

The clause ﴿You only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ is a new sentence (musta'nafah) brought to explain who benefits from the warning. The meaning of ﴿fear their Lord unseen﴾ is that they fear Him while they are absent from His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is unseen by them, or they fear Him in private, away from people.

Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is that your warning only benefits those who fear their Lord, so you warn them and not others who will not benefit from the warning, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and His saying: ﴿You only warn the one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11]. The meaning of ﴿and establish prayer﴾ is that they took great care with it and did not busy themselves away from it with anything that distracts them. ﴿And whoever purifies himself, he purifies only for himself﴾. Tazakki means purifying oneself from the filth of polytheism and immoralities. The meaning: whoever purifies himself by abandoning sins and increases in righteous deeds, he purifies only for himself, because the benefit of that is specific to him, just as the burden of whoever defiles himself falls only upon him and not upon another.

The majority read ﴿whoever purifies himself, he purifies﴾. Abu 'Amr read "yazzakki" with the ta' assimilated into the za'. Ibn Mas'ud and Talhah read "wa-man izzakka fa-innama yuzakki." ﴿And to God is the final return﴾, not to anyone else.

He, glory be to Him, first mentioned that no one bears the sin of another. Then He mentioned, second, that the sinner, if he calls another, even a relative, to bear some of his sins, that one will not bear it. Then He mentioned, third, that the reward for obedience is specific to its doer; none of it belongs to anyone else.

Then He struck a parable for the believer and the disbeliever, saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not equal﴾, that is, the one deprived of the faculty of sight and the seeing one who possesses the faculty of sight. So He likened the disbeliever to the blind and the believer to the seeing.

﴿Nor are darknesses and light﴾, that is, darknesses and light are not equal. So He likened falsehood to darknesses and truth to light.

Al-Akhfash said: the lam (wa-la) in His saying ﴿nor the light﴾ and ﴿nor the heat﴾ is extra (za'idah), and the implied sense is: ﴿And not equal are the darknesses and the light, nor the shade and the scorching heat.﴾ Al-Harur is the intensity of the heat of the sun.

Al-Akhfash said: al-harur occurs only with the daytime sun, while al-samum occurs at night. It was also said the reverse.

Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said: al-harur occurs only at night, and al-samum occurs only in the daytime.

Al-Farra' said: al-samum occurs only in the daytime, while al-harur occurs in both. Al-Nahhas said: this is more correct.

Qutrub said: al-harur is heat, and al-zill (shade) is coolness. The meaning: the shade in which there is no heat or harm is not equal to the heat that harms.

It was said: He meant reward and punishment. Heat was called harur as an intensification of the intensity of heat, because increase in the form of a word indicates increase in meaning.

Al-Kalbi said: by the shade He meant Paradise, and by the scorching heat, the Fire.

'Ata' said: He means the shade of the night and the sun of the day.

It was said: He used the plural for darknesses and the singular for light because the kinds of falsehood are many while truth is one.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another parable for the believer and the disbeliever, saying: ﴿Nor are the living and the dead equal﴾. So He likened the believers to the living and the disbelievers to the dead. It was also said: He meant the parable of scholars and the ignorant.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the living are the intelligent and the dead are the ignorant.

Qatadah said: all of these are parables, meaning: just as these things are not equal, so too the disbeliever and the believer are not equal. ﴿Indeed, God makes hear whom He wills﴾ from among His friends whom He created for His Paradise, guided to His obedience, ﴿and you cannot make hear those in the graves﴾, meaning the disbelievers whom disbelief has caused their hearts to die. That is: just as you cannot make hear one who has died, so you cannot make hear one whose heart has died.

(p-١٢١٠) The majority read "mus'mi'" with tanwin and separated from the annexation. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, and 'Amr ibn Maymun read it with annexation.

﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is, you are only a messenger who warns; upon you is only the warning and the conveyance, and guidance and misguidance are in the hand of God, mighty and majestic.

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾. Bil-haqq may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject, meaning "truthfully," or from the object, meaning "one who is made true," or as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a sending conjoined with the truth." Or it may be connected to bashiran (as a bringer of good news), meaning a bringer of good news with the true promise and a warner with the true promise. The better view is that it is a qualifier of the omitted verbal noun, so that bashiran means: a bringer of good news to the people of obedience and a warner to the people of disobedience.

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾, that is, there is no nation of the past nations but that a warner from among the prophets passed among them to warn it. He mentioned only the warner and not the bringer of good news, because it is more fitting to the context.

Then He consoled His Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, and comforted him, saying: ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had already denied﴾, that is, those nations of the past denied their prophets, whose messengers came to them ﴿with clear proofs﴾, that is, with evident miracles and manifest signs, ﴿and with scriptures﴾, that is, written books, like the scrolls of Ibrahim, ﴿and with the illuminating Book﴾, like the Torah and the Gospel. It was said: the illuminating Book is included under the scriptures and under the clear proofs, and the conjunction indicates the difference of concepts, even though they are identical in truthfulness. The better view is to restrict the clear proofs to miracles, the scriptures to books containing admonitions, and the Book to that which contains laws and rulings.

﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved﴾. Placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates explicit condemnation of them by what is in the relative clause, and points to the cause of the seizing. ﴿So how was My denial﴾, that is, how was My rejection of them and My punishment of them. Warsh, from Nafi', and Shaybah read with the yā' affirmed in "nakir" both in continuation and in pause. The explanation of this meaning has already passed recently.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Beware, no offender offends except against himself. A father does not offend against his child, nor a child against his father."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abu Ramthah, who said: "I set out with my father toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When he saw me, he said to my father: 'Is this your son?' He said: 'Yes, by the Lord of the Ka'bah.' He said: 'As for him, he will not offend against you, nor will you offend against him.' Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried﴾, that he said: "There will be upon him a burden, and he will not find anyone to carry any of his burden for him."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the neediness of His creatures toward Him and their great need for His bounty, and said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward God﴾, that is, those in need of Him in all matters of the religion and the world, so they are poor toward Him absolutely. ﴿And God is the Rich﴾, absolutely, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the one deserving praise from His servants for His kindness toward them.

﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾, that is, it is not impossible or hard for Him. The explanation of this has already passed in Surat Ibrahim.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 3):

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned a kind of His overwhelming power and a creation of His wondrous creatures, so He said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. This seeing is the seeing of the heart, meaning "Have you not known?" *Anna* (that) with its noun and predicate takes the place of the two objects. ﴿And We bring forth thereby﴾, meaning by the water. The point of this shift (*iltifat*, a change from third-person reference to first-person) is to show the complete care given to the action, because of the wondrous making it contains. The accusative of ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ (its colours being diverse) is in apposition as a description of *thamarat* (fruits). The word *alwan* (colours) here means kinds and varieties: some are white, some are red, some are yellow, some are green, and some are black. ﴿And of the mountains are streaks (judad), white and red, of diverse colours﴾. *Judad* is the plural of *juddah*, which means a path.

Al-Akhfash said: If it were the plural of *jadid*, it would have been *judud* with a *damma* on the *jim* and the *dal*, like *sarir* and *surur*. Zuhayr said:

"As if he, with blackened cheeks, having streaks, flew, and grazes at times after the summer."

It was also said: *judud* means pieces, derived from *jaddadtu al-shay'* when you cut the thing. Ibn Bahr transmitted this.

Al-Jawhari said: *Juddah* is the mark on the back of a donkey that differs in colour from the rest of it. *Juddah* also means a line or streak, and its plural is *judad* and *jada'id*. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Dark-backed, having four streaks."

Al-Mubarrad said: *judud* means lines and stripes.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said similar things in explaining *judud*.

Al-Farra' said: They are paths in the mountains, like veins, white, black and red, and their singular is *juddah*.

The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) informed us about the streaks of the mountains, which are their paths, or the lines in them, that the colour of some of them is white and the colour of some of them is red. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿white and red, of diverse colours﴾. The majority of readers read *judadun* with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *fatha* on the *dal*.

Al-Zuhri read it with a *damma* on both, as the plural of *jadidah*. It is narrated from him that he read it with a *fatha* on both. Abu Hatim rejected this reading, while others considered it sound and said: *judud* means a clear and evident path.

﴿And black, intensely black (ghara-bib sud)﴾. *Gharibib* means very intensely black, the blackness of which resembles the colour of a crow. Al-Jawhari said: You say *hadha aswad gharibib*, meaning very intensely black. If you say *gharabib sud*, you make *sud* a substitute (*badal*) for *gharabib*.

Al-Farra' said: There is an inversion in the speech; its estimated form is *wa sudun gharabib*, because it is said *aswad gharibib*, and it is rarely said *gharibib aswad*. The words ﴿of diverse colours﴾ are a description of *judad*. The words ﴿and black, intensely black﴾ are conjoined to *judad*, with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red, and of the mountains are intensely black ones, of one colour, which is black." Or they are conjoined to *humr* (red), with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red and black."

It was also said that it is conjoined to *bid* (white), and there must be an omitted possessive construction before *judad*, meaning "and of the mountains is one with streaks," because the streaks are only in the colours of some of them.

﴿And of mankind and the moving creatures and cattle, of diverse colours likewise﴾. The word *mukhtalif* (diverse) is a description of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among them is a kind, or a type, or a part, of diverse colours, by red, black, white, green and yellow."

Al-Farra' said: That is, a creation ﴿of diverse colours﴾ like the diversity of fruits and mountains. Allah (glory be to Him) mentioned the diversity of colours in these things because this diversity is among the greatest proofs of Allah's power and wondrous making.

The meaning of *kadhalika* (likewise) is: diverse in a way like that diversity, and it is a description of an omitted verbal noun. The estimated form is "diverse in colours in a diversity existing likewise," meaning like the diversity of mountains and fruits.

Al-Zuhri read *wad-dawabbi* (and the moving creatures) with the *ba'* lightened (without doubling). Ibn al-Sumayfa read *alwanuha* (its colours).

It was also said that *kadhalika* is connected to what follows it, meaning: "Likewise, the rain, and the consideration of Allah's creatures and the diversity of their colours; among His servants, the scholars fear Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this, but it is rejected, because what comes after *inna* does not operate on what comes before it.

The preferred view is the first, and stopping at *kadhalika* is complete.

Then the speech is resumed, and He (glory be to Him) informed us with His words: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. Or it is part of His words: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18], with the meaning: only those who know Him fear Him (glory be to Him) unseen, and know what befits Him of His majestic attributes and beautiful acts. In every case, He (glory be to Him) has specified in this verse the people of His fear, and they are those who know Him and magnify His power.

Mujahid said: The scholar is only one who fears Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Masruq said: Fear of Allah is enough knowledge, and self-delusion is enough ignorance. Whoever knows Allah most, is most fearful of Him.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Whoever does not fear Allah is not a scholar.

Al-Sha'bi said: The scholar is one who fears Allah.

The reason for placing the object first (*ta'khir*, i.e. *taqdim al-maf'ul*) is that the context is a context of restricting the agency (*hasr al-fa'iliyyah*). If it were postponed, the matter would be reversed.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz read the noble name (Allah) in the nominative and *al-'ulama'* (the scholars) in the accusative, and this reading was narrated from Abu Hanifa. Al-Zamakhshari said in the *Kashshaf*: "Fear" in this reading is a metaphor, and the meaning is that He honours and magnifies them as a dreaded and awe-inspiring man is held in awe among people.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving﴾ is a reason for the obligation of fear, indicating that He punishes for disobedience to Him, and forgives whoever of His servants repents.

﴿Indeed those who recite the Book of Allah﴾, meaning they continue in its recitation and persist in it. The Book is the Noble Qur'an, and there is no basis for what is said, that what is meant by it is the category of the books of Allah. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning they perform it at its times with full pillars and remembrances. ﴿And spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. In this is an exhortation to spend in whatever way is possible: if it is possible secretly, that is better, and otherwise openly. Suspicion that it may be ostentation does not prevent it. It is possible that by secrecy is meant voluntary charity, and by openness obligatory charity.

The clause ﴿They hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ is in the place of nominative as the predicate of *inna*, as Tha'lab and others said.
