Zirr ibn Hubaysh and al-Tirmidhi read جَنَّةُ (jannah, singular). Al-Jahdari read جَنّاتٍ (jannatin) in the accusative, as an object construction (ishtighal). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that جَنّاتُ be a second predicate of the demonstrative. Abu 'Amr read يُدْخَلُونَها (yudkhalunaha) in the passive voice. The word يُحَلَّوْنَ (yuhallawna, "they will be adorned") is a second predicate of "Gardens of Eden", or a circumstantial clause (hal) that is understood. It derives from حَلِيَتِ المَرْأةُ (haliyati al-mar'ah, "the woman adorned herself with jewellery"). In it is an indication of speed of entry, for adorning them outside Paradise would delay their entry. So when He said يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيها ("they will be adorned therein"), He indicated that their entry will be swift. The "min" in مِن أساوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ: the first (min in "min asawira") is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the second (min in "min dhahab") is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: they will be adorned with some bracelets made of gold. Asawir is the plural of أسْوِرَة, the plural of siwar (bracelet). The accusative of لُؤْلُؤًا (lu'lu'an, "pearls") is by coordination with the position (mahall) of مِن أساوِرَ. It was also read in the genitive, coordinated with ذَهَبٍ. ﴿Their clothing therein is silk﴾: the interpretation of this verse has been fully given in Surah al-Hajj.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief"﴾. The majority read الحَزَنَ (al-hazan) with two fatahs. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay (al-huzn).

The meaning is that they will say this statement when they enter Paradise. Qatadah said: "Grief of death." 'Ikrimah said: "Grief over misdeeds and sins, and fear that their acts of obedience will be rejected." Al-Qasim said: "Grief over the loss of blessings and fear of the outcome." It was said: "Grief over the terrors of the Day of Resurrection." Al-Kalbi said: "What used to grieve them in the world concerning the matter of the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The concern for bread in this world." It was said: "The concern for livelihood."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah has removed from the people of Paradise all griefs, whether they were about livelihood or about the Hereafter."

This is the most preferred of the sayings, for the world, however great its pleasures, is not free of impurities and calamities, which cause many griefs, especially for the people of faith. They are always fearful of the punishment of Allah, afraid of His retribution, with hearts in turmoil at every moment, wondering: will their deeds be accepted or rejected? Fearful of the evil end and the bad conclusion. Then their concerns and griefs do not cease until they enter Paradise.

As for the people of disobedience: although their stranglehold may be loosened a little in the life of this world, which is the abode of delusion, and although they forget the abode of permanence for a time of their lives, their dread will certainly intensify and their calamity will grow, and the cauldrons of their griefs will boil when they approach death and draw near the abodes of the Hereafter. Then, when their souls are taken and what displeases them of the recompense for their deeds appears to them, their sorrow and grief increase. But if Allah bestows His favour upon them with forgiveness and admits them into Paradise, then He has removed their griefs and dispelled their sorrows and concerns. ﴿Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, meaning: Forgiving to whoever disobeys Him, and Appreciative to whoever obeys Him.

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty﴾, meaning the abode of residence in which one remains forever and from which one is never removed, by His grace and mercy. ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, meaning: no hardship, toil or difficulty will afflict us in Paradise. ﴿And no weariness touches us therein﴾: al-lughub is exhaustion from toil, and al-kalal is weariness from fatigue.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾: "White, red and black." And concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "White streaks," meaning colours.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "Gharabib (in His saying 'and jet-black') means the intensely black."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "Streaks that exist in the mountain, white and red; these are the streaks." ﴿And jet-black﴾: "Black mountains." And concerning the people, the animals and the cattle he said: "Likewise is the diversity of people, animals and cattle, like the diversity of mountains." Then he said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "This is a separation from what precedes it."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the verse ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "The scholars of Allah, who fear Him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning the verse: "Those who know that Allah is capable of everything."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Adi related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Knowledge does not come from much narration; rather, knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tabarani related from him, who said: "Fear of Allah is sufficient as knowledge, and being deceived about Allah is sufficient as ignorance."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd also related from him: "Knowledge does not come from abundance of narration, but knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Hudhayfah, who said: "It is enough for the believer of knowledge that he fears Allah."

'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi related in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that Husayn ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf was the one concerning whom ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer﴾ was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾: "They are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah made them inherit every Book that was revealed. So their wrongdoer to himself is forgiven, their moderate is held to a light account, and their foremost enters Paradise without reckoning."

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he "said concerning this verse: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ — he said: 'All of these are on one level, and all of them will enter Paradise.'" In its chain are two unknown men.

Imam Ahmad said in his Musnad: He said: "Shu'bah narrated to us from al-Walid ibn al-'Ayzar, that he heard a man from Thaqif narrating from a man from Kinanah, from Abu Sa'id."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by Allah's permission﴾. As for those who were foremost, they are the ones who enter Paradise without reckoning. As for those who were moderate, they will be held to a light account. As for those who wronged themselves, they will be detained for a long time at the gathering place, and then they are the ones whom Allah will overlook by His mercy. They are the ones who will say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ to the end of the verse.'"

Al-Bayhaqi said: "When narrations for a hadith multiply, it shows that the hadith has a basis." End of quote. In the chain of Ahmad is Muhammad ibn Ishaq. In the chain of Ibn Abi Hatim is an unknown man, for he narrated it through al-A'mash from a man, from Abu Thabit, from Abu al-Darda'. Ibn Jarir narrated it from al-A'mash, who said: "Abu Thabit mentioned it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from 'Awf ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "My Ummah is in three thirds: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be held to a light account and then enter Paradise, and a third will be purified and examined, and then the angels will come and say: 'We found them saying: There is no god but Allah alone.' Allah will say: 'Admit them into Paradise because of their saying: There is no god but Allah alone, and place their sins upon the people of denial.' And these are what Allah refers to in His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 13]." And its confirmation is in what was mentioned concerning the angels.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾, and so He made them three groups.

﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾: this is the one who is examined and purified. ﴿And among them is one who is moderate﴾: this is the one who is held to a light account. ﴿And among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾: this is the one who enters Paradise without reckoning or punishment, by Allah's permission; they all enter it.

Ibn Kathir said after mentioning this hadith: "Very strange." End of quote.

Some of these hadiths strengthen one another, and they must be accepted. Through them the view of those who understood "the one who wrongs himself" as the disbeliever is refuted. They are supported by what al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Usamah ibn Zayd concerning ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of them are from this Ummah, and all of them are in Paradise." And by what al-Tayalisi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Uqbah ibn Sihban, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What do you say about the saying of Allah: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾ and so on?' She said: 'As for the foremost, they are those who lived during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he testified for them to Paradise. As for the moderate, they are those who followed their traces and acted like their deeds until they joined them. As for the one who wrongs himself, he is like me and you, and whoever follows us, and all are in Paradise.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "This Ummah on the Day of Resurrection is in three thirds: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be reckoned with an easy reckoning, and a third will come with great sins, but they do not associate partners with God. The Lord will say: 'Admit these into the expanse of My mercy.' Then he recited: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ – the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that whenever he recited this verse, ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾, he would say: "Verily, our foremost is foremost, our moderate one is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven."

Al-Uqayli, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated it through another chain from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn al-Najjar narrated it from the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The foremost in good deeds enters Paradise without reckoning, the moderate one enters Paradise by the mercy of God, and the one who wrongs himself and the people of al-A'raf enter Paradise by the intercession of Muhammad – may God bless him and his family and grant him peace."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Uthman ibn Affan that he recited this verse, then said: "Verily, our foremost are the people of our jihad; verily, our moderate ones are the people of our settled areas; and verily, our wrongdoers are the people of our desert."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from al-Bara' ibn Azib, regarding His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ – the verse, that he said: "I bear witness before God that He will admit them all into Paradise."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (al-Bara') that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ and said: 'All of them are saved, and they are this Ummah.'"

Al-Firyabi and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It is like the one in al-Waqi'ah: ﴿the companions of the right hand and the companions of the left hand﴾. And the foremost are two saved groups and one destroyed group."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ that he said: "He is the disbeliever, and the moderate ones are the companions of the right hand."

This report transmitted from him (may God be pleased with him) does not agree with the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, nor does it accord with the narrations we have already mentioned from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b about this verse, and he said: "They all are saved." Then he said: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, their shoulders have touched (in Paradise); then they are given the bounty according to their deeds." We have already mentioned from Ibn Abbas what indicates that the one who wrongs himself is among the saved, so the reports from him conflict.

al-Tirmidhi, and al-Hakim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) "recited God's saying: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, they will enter them; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾, and said: 'Upon them will be crowns; the smallest pearl among them would illuminate what lies between the east and the west.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: All praise is for God﴾ – the verse, that he said: "They are a people in this world who fear God and strive hard in worship, openly and secretly, and in their hearts is sorrow over sins they committed earlier. So they fear that this striving will not be accepted from them because of the earlier sins. Then they say: ﴿All praise is for God, who has removed from us the grief; indeed our Lord is Forgiving, Appreciative﴾ – He forgave us the great (sins) and appreciated from us the little of our deeds."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim who authenticated it narrated from him regarding the verse that he said: "(The grief) is the grief of the Fire."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 3):

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned a kind of His overwhelming power and a creation of His wondrous creatures, so He said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. This seeing is the seeing of the heart, meaning "Have you not known?" *Anna* (that) with its noun and predicate takes the place of the two objects. ﴿And We bring forth thereby﴾, meaning by the water. The point of this shift (*iltifat*, a change from third-person reference to first-person) is to show the complete care given to the action, because of the wondrous making it contains. The accusative of ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ (its colours being diverse) is in apposition as a description of *thamarat* (fruits). The word *alwan* (colours) here means kinds and varieties: some are white, some are red, some are yellow, some are green, and some are black. ﴿And of the mountains are streaks (judad), white and red, of diverse colours﴾. *Judad* is the plural of *juddah*, which means a path.

Al-Akhfash said: If it were the plural of *jadid*, it would have been *judud* with a *damma* on the *jim* and the *dal*, like *sarir* and *surur*. Zuhayr said:

"As if he, with blackened cheeks, having streaks, flew, and grazes at times after the summer."

It was also said: *judud* means pieces, derived from *jaddadtu al-shay'* when you cut the thing. Ibn Bahr transmitted this.

Al-Jawhari said: *Juddah* is the mark on the back of a donkey that differs in colour from the rest of it. *Juddah* also means a line or streak, and its plural is *judad* and *jada'id*. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Dark-backed, having four streaks."

Al-Mubarrad said: *judud* means lines and stripes.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said similar things in explaining *judud*.

Al-Farra' said: They are paths in the mountains, like veins, white, black and red, and their singular is *juddah*.

The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) informed us about the streaks of the mountains, which are their paths, or the lines in them, that the colour of some of them is white and the colour of some of them is red. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿white and red, of diverse colours﴾. The majority of readers read *judadun* with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *fatha* on the *dal*.

Al-Zuhri read it with a *damma* on both, as the plural of *jadidah*. It is narrated from him that he read it with a *fatha* on both. Abu Hatim rejected this reading, while others considered it sound and said: *judud* means a clear and evident path.

﴿And black, intensely black (ghara-bib sud)﴾. *Gharibib* means very intensely black, the blackness of which resembles the colour of a crow. Al-Jawhari said: You say *hadha aswad gharibib*, meaning very intensely black. If you say *gharabib sud*, you make *sud* a substitute (*badal*) for *gharabib*.

Al-Farra' said: There is an inversion in the speech; its estimated form is *wa sudun gharabib*, because it is said *aswad gharibib*, and it is rarely said *gharibib aswad*. The words ﴿of diverse colours﴾ are a description of *judad*. The words ﴿and black, intensely black﴾ are conjoined to *judad*, with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red, and of the mountains are intensely black ones, of one colour, which is black." Or they are conjoined to *humr* (red), with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red and black."

It was also said that it is conjoined to *bid* (white), and there must be an omitted possessive construction before *judad*, meaning "and of the mountains is one with streaks," because the streaks are only in the colours of some of them.

﴿And of mankind and the moving creatures and cattle, of diverse colours likewise﴾. The word *mukhtalif* (diverse) is a description of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among them is a kind, or a type, or a part, of diverse colours, by red, black, white, green and yellow."

Al-Farra' said: That is, a creation ﴿of diverse colours﴾ like the diversity of fruits and mountains. Allah (glory be to Him) mentioned the diversity of colours in these things because this diversity is among the greatest proofs of Allah's power and wondrous making.

The meaning of *kadhalika* (likewise) is: diverse in a way like that diversity, and it is a description of an omitted verbal noun. The estimated form is "diverse in colours in a diversity existing likewise," meaning like the diversity of mountains and fruits.

Al-Zuhri read *wad-dawabbi* (and the moving creatures) with the *ba'* lightened (without doubling). Ibn al-Sumayfa read *alwanuha* (its colours).

It was also said that *kadhalika* is connected to what follows it, meaning: "Likewise, the rain, and the consideration of Allah's creatures and the diversity of their colours; among His servants, the scholars fear Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this, but it is rejected, because what comes after *inna* does not operate on what comes before it.

The preferred view is the first, and stopping at *kadhalika* is complete.

Then the speech is resumed, and He (glory be to Him) informed us with His words: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. Or it is part of His words: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18], with the meaning: only those who know Him fear Him (glory be to Him) unseen, and know what befits Him of His majestic attributes and beautiful acts. In every case, He (glory be to Him) has specified in this verse the people of His fear, and they are those who know Him and magnify His power.

Mujahid said: The scholar is only one who fears Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Masruq said: Fear of Allah is enough knowledge, and self-delusion is enough ignorance. Whoever knows Allah most, is most fearful of Him.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Whoever does not fear Allah is not a scholar.

Al-Sha'bi said: The scholar is one who fears Allah.

The reason for placing the object first (*ta'khir*, i.e. *taqdim al-maf'ul*) is that the context is a context of restricting the agency (*hasr al-fa'iliyyah*). If it were postponed, the matter would be reversed.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz read the noble name (Allah) in the nominative and *al-'ulama'* (the scholars) in the accusative, and this reading was narrated from Abu Hanifa. Al-Zamakhshari said in the *Kashshaf*: "Fear" in this reading is a metaphor, and the meaning is that He honours and magnifies them as a dreaded and awe-inspiring man is held in awe among people.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving﴾ is a reason for the obligation of fear, indicating that He punishes for disobedience to Him, and forgives whoever of His servants repents.

﴿Indeed those who recite the Book of Allah﴾, meaning they continue in its recitation and persist in it. The Book is the Noble Qur'an, and there is no basis for what is said, that what is meant by it is the category of the books of Allah. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning they perform it at its times with full pillars and remembrances. ﴿And spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. In this is an exhortation to spend in whatever way is possible: if it is possible secretly, that is better, and otherwise openly. Suspicion that it may be ostentation does not prevent it. It is possible that by secrecy is meant voluntary charity, and by openness obligatory charity.

The clause ﴿They hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ is in the place of nominative as the predicate of *inna*, as Tha'lab and others said. What is meant by commerce is the reward for obedience. The meaning of ﴿will never perish﴾ is will never become dull or be destroyed. It is a description of the commerce. The informing about their hope for the reward of what they did is in the position of a promise that their hoped-for thing will be attained.

The *lam* in ﴿that He may pay them their rewards﴾ is connected to ﴿will never perish﴾, with the meaning: that it will not become dull for the sake of paying them the rewards of their righteous deeds. A similar verse is His words (glory be to Him): ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nisa': 173]. It was also said that the *lam* is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, meaning: they did that so that He might pay them. The meaning of ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾ is that He bestows upon them an increase beyond their rewards, which are the recompense for their deeds.

The clause ﴿Indeed He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is a reason for what was mentioned of full payment and increase, meaning: He forgives their sins and appreciates their obedience. It was also said that this clause is the predicate of *inna*, and the clause ﴿they hope﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The first is preferable.

﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ refers to the Qur'an. It was also said it refers to the Preserved Tablet, with *min* being partitive or initial (indicating origin). The clause ﴿is the truth﴾ is the predicate of the relative pronoun. ﴿Confirming what is before it﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: agreeing with the books that came before it. ﴿Indeed Allah is, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾, meaning: encompassing all their affairs.

﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾. The first object of *awrathna* (We caused to inherit) is the relative pronoun, and the second object is *al-kitab* (the Book). The second object was placed first to honour and magnify the Book. The meaning is: "Then We caused those whom We chose from among Our servants to inherit the Book," which is the Qur'an. That is: We decreed and ordained that We would make the scholars of your community, O Muhammad, inherit this Book which We revealed to you. The meaning of their being chosen is their being selected and singled out. There is no doubt that the scholars of this community, from the Companions onward, have been honoured by Allah above all other servants. He made them a middle community so that they might be witnesses over mankind, and He honoured them by making them the community of the best of prophets and the master of the children of Adam (ﷺ).

Muqatil said: He means the Qur'an of Muhammad; We made it reach those whom We chose from among Our servants.

It was also said that the meaning is: We caused it to be inherited from the earlier nations, that is, We delayed it from them and gave it to those whom We chose. The first view is preferable.

Then He (glory be to Him) divided those whom He caused to inherit His Book and whom He chose from among His servants into three categories, so He said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾. Many people of knowledge have found the meaning of this verse problematic, because He (glory be to Him) made this category, the one who wrongs himself, part of that division, namely those whom He chose from among the servants. So how can one whom Allah has chosen be one who wrongs himself? It was said: the division refers to the servants, meaning: among Our servants is one who wrongs himself, and this is the disbeliever, and the pronoun in ﴿they will enter it﴾ refers to the moderate one and the foremost.

It was also said: What is meant by the one who wrongs himself is the one who falls short in acting upon it, and he is the one whose matter is deferred to Allah's command. It is not necessarily the case that the inheritors of the Book observe it with its full observance, because of His words: ﴿Then there succeeded them a later generation who inherited the Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]. This is open to question, because wronging oneself does not fit with being chosen.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who committed minor sins. This view has been narrated from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda' and 'A'isha. This is the preferred view, because committing minor sins does not contradict being chosen, nor does it prevent its doer from entering Paradise with those who enter it: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾, and so on to the end of what will come.

The sense in which he is one who wrongs himself is that he diminished his own reward by the minor sins he committed, which are forgiven for him. If he had done good deeds instead of those minor sins, he would have had a great share of reward for himself. It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who commits major sins.

The early scholars differed in explaining the foremost (*al-sabiq*) and the moderate (*al-muqtasid*). 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious one without qualification. This is also what al-Farra' said. Mujahid said in explaining the verse: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ refers to the companions of the left hand; ﴿and among them is one who is moderate﴾ refers to the companions of the right hand; ﴿and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ refers to the foremost of all people.

Al-Mubarrad said: the moderate is one who gives the world its due and the Hereafter its due.

Al-Hasan said: the one who wrongs himself is the one whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds; the moderate is the one whose good and evil deeds are equal; the foremost is the one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds.

Muqatil said: the one who wrongs himself is the people of major sins among the people of monotheism; the moderate is the one who has not committed a major sin; and the foremost is the one who hastened to righteous deeds.

Al-Nahhas reported that the one who wrongs himself is the owner of major sins, and the moderate is the one who did not deserve Paradise by having his good deeds outweigh his evil deeds, so the Gardens of Eden which they enter are for "those who hastened to good deeds" only. He said: This is the view of a group of people of reflection, because the pronoun in the true sense of reflection refers to what is nearest to it, which is preferable.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, meaning: among their descendants is one who wrongs himself.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the foremost is the scholar, the moderate is the learner, and the one who wrongs himself is the ignorant.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who remembers Allah only with his tongue; the moderate is the one who remembers with his heart; and the foremost is the one who never forgets Him.

Al-Antaki said: the one who wrongs himself is the owner of words, the moderate is the owner of deeds, and the foremost is the owner of spiritual states.

Ibn 'Ata' said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who loves Allah for the sake of this world; the moderate is the one who loves Allah for the sake of the reward in the Hereafter; and the foremost is the one who let his own desire fall away in favour of the desire of the Truth.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who worships Allah out of fear of the Fire; the moderate is the one who worships Him out of hope for Paradise; and the foremost is the one who worships Him without any cause.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who loves himself; the moderate is the one who loves his religion; and the foremost is the one who loves his Lord.

Some said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who takes his share (of the world) but does not give others their due. The moderate one (al-muqtasid) is the one who takes his share and gives others their due. The foremost (al-sabiq) is the one who gives others their due and does not take his share.

Al-Tha'labi and others have mentioned many sayings. There is no doubt that the linguistic meanings of "the wrongdoer" (al-zalim), "the moderate" (al-muqtasid) and "the foremost" (al-sabiq) are well known, and that the wrongdoer to himself is one who simply deprives himself of his benefit and loses what is better for him. So one who does not multiply acts of obedience has wronged himself in terms of the reward he has forfeited, even though he performs what Allah has made obligatory for him and avoids what Allah has forbidden. From this aspect, he is among those whom Allah has chosen and among the people of Paradise, so there is no difficulty in the verse. From this is the saying of Adam: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [Al-A'raf: 23], and the saying of Yunus: ﴿Indeed, I was among the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 87]. The meaning of the moderate is one who takes a middle course in matters of religion, inclining neither to excess nor to negligence, and this one is among the people of Paradise. As for the foremost, he is the one who surpasses others in matters of religion, and he is the best of the three.

The placing of the wrongdoer before the moderate, and of both before the foremost, has been raised as a difficulty, given that the moderate is better than the wrongdoer to himself and the foremost is better than both. It was said that mention order does not necessarily imply honour, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal﴾ [Al-Hashr: 20], and similar Qur'anic verses in which the people of evil are mentioned before the people of good, and the less excellent are mentioned before the more excellent.

It was also said that the reason for the order here is that the moderate, in relation to the people of disobedience, are few, and the foremost, in relation to both groups, are fewer still; so the more numerous is placed before the less numerous. The first answer is preferable, for numerical abundance alone does not require earlier mention. Other reasons for the order have been given besides what we have mentioned, and there is no need to lengthen the discussion with them.

The reference in His saying "that" (dhalika) is to the inheritance of the Book and the choosing. It was said that it refers to the race to good deeds, but the first is preferable. It (dhalika) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "the great bounty", meaning the bounty whose extent cannot be measured.

The phrase ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is in the nominative either as a subject (mubtada') with what follows it as its predicate (khabar), or as an apposition (badal) to "the bounty", because it is the cause of attaining the reward and so has been treated as the one that causes it. On this view, the clause ﴿they will enter them﴾ is a new sentence (musta'nafah). We have already said that the pronoun in ﴿they will enter them﴾ refers to the three categories, so there is no basis for restricting it to the last category.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh and al-Tirmidhi read جَنَّةُ (jannah, singular). Al-Jahdari read جَنّاتٍ (jannatin) in the accusative, as an object construction (ishtighal). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that جَنّاتُ be a second predicate of the demonstrative. Abu 'Amr read يُدْخَلُونَها (yudkhalunaha) in the passive voice. The word يُحَلَّوْنَ (yuhallawna, "they will be adorned") is a second predicate of "Gardens of Eden", or a circumstantial clause (hal) that is understood. It derives from حَلِيَتِ المَرْأةُ (haliyati al-mar'ah, "the woman adorned herself with jewellery"). In it is an indication of speed of entry, for adorning them outside Paradise would delay their entry. So when He said يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيها ("they will be adorned therein"), He indicated that their entry will be swift. The "min" in مِن أساوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ: the first (min in "min asawira") is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the second (min in "min dhahab") is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: they will be adorned with some bracelets made of gold. Asawir is the plural of أسْوِرَة, the plural of siwar (bracelet). The accusative of لُؤْلُؤًا (lu'lu'an, "pearls") is by coordination with the position (mahall) of مِن أساوِرَ. It was also read in the genitive, coordinated with ذَهَبٍ. ﴿Their clothing therein is silk﴾: the interpretation of this verse has been fully given in Surah al-Hajj.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief"﴾. The majority read الحَزَنَ (al-hazan) with two fatahs. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay (al-huzn).

The meaning is that they will say this statement when they enter Paradise. Qatadah said: "Grief of death." 'Ikrimah said: "Grief over misdeeds and sins, and fear that their acts of obedience will be rejected." Al-Qasim said: "Grief over the loss of blessings and fear of the outcome." It was said: "Grief over the terrors of the Day of Resurrection." Al-Kalbi said: "What used to grieve them in the world concerning the matter of the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The concern for bread in this world." It was said: "The concern for livelihood."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah has removed from the people of Paradise all griefs, whether they were about livelihood or about the Hereafter."

This is the most preferred of the sayings, for the world, however great its pleasures, is not free of impurities and calamities, which cause many griefs, especially for the people of faith. They are always fearful of the punishment of Allah, afraid of His retribution, with hearts in turmoil at every moment, wondering: will their deeds be accepted or rejected? Fearful of the evil end and the bad conclusion. Then their concerns and griefs do not cease until they enter Paradise.

As for the people of disobedience: although their stranglehold may be loosened a little in the life of this world, which is the abode of delusion, and although they forget the abode of permanence for a time of their lives, their dread will certainly intensify and their calamity will grow, and the cauldrons of their griefs will boil when they approach death and draw near the abodes of the Hereafter. Then, when their souls are taken and what displeases them of the recompense for their deeds appears to them, their sorrow and grief increase. But if Allah bestows His favour upon them with forgiveness and admits them into Paradise, then He has removed their griefs and dispelled their sorrows and concerns. ﴿Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, meaning: Forgiving to whoever disobeys Him, and Appreciative to whoever obeys Him.

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty﴾, meaning the abode of residence in which one remains forever and from which one is never removed, by His grace and mercy. ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, meaning: no hardship, toil or difficulty will afflict us in Paradise. ﴿And no weariness touches us therein﴾: al-lughub is exhaustion from toil, and al-kalal is weariness from fatigue.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾: "White, red and black." And concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "White streaks," meaning colours.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "Gharabib (in His saying 'and jet-black') means the intensely black."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "Streaks that exist in the mountain, white and red; these are the streaks." ﴿And jet-black﴾: "Black mountains." And concerning the people, the animals and the cattle he said: "Likewise is the diversity of people, animals and cattle, like the diversity of mountains." Then he said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "This is a separation from what precedes it."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the verse ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "The scholars of Allah, who fear Him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning the verse: "Those who know that Allah is capable of everything."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Adi related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Knowledge does not come from much narration; rather, knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tabarani related from him, who said: "Fear of Allah is sufficient as knowledge, and being deceived about Allah is sufficient as ignorance."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd also related from him: "Knowledge does not come from abundance of narration, but knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Hudhayfah, who said: "It is enough for the believer of knowledge that he fears Allah."

'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi related in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that Husayn ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf was the one concerning whom ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer﴾ was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾: "They are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah made them inherit every Book that was revealed. So their wrongdoer to himself is forgiven, their moderate is held to a light account, and their foremost enters Paradise without reckoning."

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he "said concerning this verse: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ — he said: 'All of these are on one level, and all of them will enter Paradise.'" In its chain are two unknown men.

Imam Ahmad said in his Musnad: He said: "Shu'bah narrated to us from al-Walid ibn al-'Ayzar, that he heard a man from Thaqif narrating from a man from Kinanah, from Abu Sa'id."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by Allah's permission﴾. As for those who were foremost, they are the ones who enter Paradise without reckoning. As for those who were moderate, they will be held to a light account. As for those who wronged themselves, they will be detained for a long time at the gathering place, and then they are the ones whom Allah will overlook by His mercy. They are the ones who will say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ to the end of the verse.'"

Al-Bayhaqi said: "When narrations for a hadith multiply, it shows that the hadith has a basis." End of quote. In the chain of Ahmad is Muhammad ibn Ishaq. In the chain of Ibn Abi Hatim is an unknown man, for he narrated it through al-A'mash from a man, from Abu Thabit, from Abu al-Darda'. Ibn Jarir narrated it from al-A'mash, who said: "Abu Thabit mentioned it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from 'Awf ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "My Ummah is in three thirds: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be held to a light account and then enter Paradise, and a third will be purified and examined, and then the angels will come and say: 'We found them saying: There is no god but Allah alone.' Allah will say: 'Admit them into Paradise because of their saying: There is no god but Allah alone, and place their sins upon the people of denial.' And these are what Allah refers to in His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 13]." And its confirmation is in what was mentioned concerning the angels.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾, and so He made them three groups.

﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾: this is the one who is examined and purified. ﴿And among them is one who is moderate﴾: this is the one who is held to a light account. ﴿And among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾: this is the one who enters Paradise without reckoning or punishment, by Allah's permission; they all enter it.

Ibn Kathir said after mentioning this hadith: "Very strange." End of quote.

Some of these hadiths strengthen one another, and they must be accepted. Through them the view of those who understood "the one who wrongs himself" as the disbeliever is refuted. They are supported by what al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Usamah ibn Zayd concerning ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of them are from this Ummah, and all of them are in Paradise." And by what al-Tayalisi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Uqbah ibn Sihban, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What do you say about the saying of Allah: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾ and so on?' She said: 'As for the foremost, they are those who lived during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he testified for them to Paradise. As for the moderate, they are those who followed their traces and acted like their deeds until they joined them. As for the one who wrongs himself, he is like me and you, and whoever follows us, and all are in Paradise.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "This Ummah on the Day of Resurrection is in three thirds: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be reckoned with an easy reckoning, and a third will come with great sins, but they do not associate partners with God. The Lord will say: 'Admit these into the expanse of My mercy.' Then he recited: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ – the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that whenever he recited this verse, ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾, he would say: "Verily, our foremost is foremost, our moderate one is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven."

Al-Uqayli, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated it through another chain from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn al-Najjar narrated it from the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The foremost in good deeds enters Paradise without reckoning, the moderate one enters Paradise by the mercy of God, and the one who wrongs himself and the people of al-A'raf enter Paradise by the intercession of Muhammad – may God bless him and his family and grant him peace."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Uthman ibn Affan that he recited this verse, then said: "Verily, our foremost are the people of our jihad; verily, our moderate ones are the people of our settled areas; and verily, our wrongdoers are the people of our desert."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from al-Bara' ibn Azib, regarding His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ – the verse, that he said: "I bear witness before God that He will admit them all into Paradise."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (al-Bara') that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ and said: 'All of them are saved, and they are this Ummah.'"

Al-Firyabi and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse that he said: "It is like the one in al-Waqi'ah: ﴿the companions of the right hand and the companions of the left hand﴾. And the foremost are two saved groups and one destroyed group."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ that he said: "He is the disbeliever, and the moderate ones are the companions of the right hand."

This report transmitted from him (may God be pleased with him) does not agree with the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording, nor does it accord with the narrations we have already mentioned from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and from a group of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith that Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b about this verse, and he said: "They all are saved." Then he said: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, their shoulders have touched (in Paradise); then they are given the bounty according to their deeds." We have already mentioned from Ibn Abbas what indicates that the one who wrongs himself is among the saved, so the reports from him conflict.

al-Tirmidhi, and al-Hakim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) "recited God's saying: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, they will enter them; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾, and said: 'Upon them will be crowns; the smallest pearl among them would illuminate what lies between the east and the west.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: All praise is for God﴾ – the verse, that he said: "They are a people in this world who fear God and strive hard in worship, openly and secretly, and in their hearts is sorrow over sins they committed earlier. So they fear that this striving will not be accepted from them because of the earlier sins. Then they say: ﴿All praise is for God, who has removed from us the grief; indeed our Lord is Forgiving, Appreciative﴾ – He forgave us the great (sins) and appreciated from us the little of our deeds."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim who authenticated it narrated from him regarding the verse that he said: "(The grief) is the grief of the Fire."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 3):

Then He (glory be to Him) mentioned a kind of His overwhelming power and a creation of His wondrous creatures, so He said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. This seeing is the seeing of the heart, meaning "Have you not known?" *Anna* (that) with its noun and predicate takes the place of the two objects. ﴿And We bring forth thereby﴾, meaning by the water. The point of this shift (*iltifat*, a change from third-person reference to first-person) is to show the complete care given to the action, because of the wondrous making it contains. The accusative of ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ (its colours being diverse) is in apposition as a description of *thamarat* (fruits). The word *alwan* (colours) here means kinds and varieties: some are white, some are red, some are yellow, some are green, and some are black. ﴿And of the mountains are streaks (judad), white and red, of diverse colours﴾. *Judad* is the plural of *juddah*, which means a path.

Al-Akhfash said: If it were the plural of *jadid*, it would have been *judud* with a *damma* on the *jim* and the *dal*, like *sarir* and *surur*. Zuhayr said:

"As if he, with blackened cheeks, having streaks, flew, and grazes at times after the summer."

It was also said: *judud* means pieces, derived from *jaddadtu al-shay'* when you cut the thing. Ibn Bahr transmitted this.

Al-Jawhari said: *Juddah* is the mark on the back of a donkey that differs in colour from the rest of it. *Juddah* also means a line or streak, and its plural is *judad* and *jada'id*. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Dark-backed, having four streaks."

Al-Mubarrad said: *judud* means lines and stripes.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said similar things in explaining *judud*.

Al-Farra' said: They are paths in the mountains, like veins, white, black and red, and their singular is *juddah*.

The meaning is that Allah (glory be to Him) informed us about the streaks of the mountains, which are their paths, or the lines in them, that the colour of some of them is white and the colour of some of them is red. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿white and red, of diverse colours﴾. The majority of readers read *judadun* with a *damma* on the *jim* and a *fatha* on the *dal*.

Al-Zuhri read it with a *damma* on both, as the plural of *jadidah*. It is narrated from him that he read it with a *fatha* on both. Abu Hatim rejected this reading, while others considered it sound and said: *judud* means a clear and evident path.

﴿And black, intensely black (ghara-bib sud)﴾. *Gharibib* means very intensely black, the blackness of which resembles the colour of a crow. Al-Jawhari said: You say *hadha aswad gharibib*, meaning very intensely black. If you say *gharabib sud*, you make *sud* a substitute (*badal*) for *gharabib*.

Al-Farra' said: There is an inversion in the speech; its estimated form is *wa sudun gharabib*, because it is said *aswad gharibib*, and it is rarely said *gharibib aswad*. The words ﴿of diverse colours﴾ are a description of *judad*. The words ﴿and black, intensely black﴾ are conjoined to *judad*, with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red, and of the mountains are intensely black ones, of one colour, which is black." Or they are conjoined to *humr* (red), with the meaning: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red and black."

It was also said that it is conjoined to *bid* (white), and there must be an omitted possessive construction before *judad*, meaning "and of the mountains is one with streaks," because the streaks are only in the colours of some of them.

﴿And of mankind and the moving creatures and cattle, of diverse colours likewise﴾. The word *mukhtalif* (diverse) is a description of an omitted noun, meaning: "and among them is a kind, or a type, or a part, of diverse colours, by red, black, white, green and yellow."

Al-Farra' said: That is, a creation ﴿of diverse colours﴾ like the diversity of fruits and mountains. Allah (glory be to Him) mentioned the diversity of colours in these things because this diversity is among the greatest proofs of Allah's power and wondrous making.

The meaning of *kadhalika* (likewise) is: diverse in a way like that diversity, and it is a description of an omitted verbal noun. The estimated form is "diverse in colours in a diversity existing likewise," meaning like the diversity of mountains and fruits.

Al-Zuhri read *wad-dawabbi* (and the moving creatures) with the *ba'* lightened (without doubling). Ibn al-Sumayfa read *alwanuha* (its colours).

It was also said that *kadhalika* is connected to what follows it, meaning: "Likewise, the rain, and the consideration of Allah's creatures and the diversity of their colours; among His servants, the scholars fear Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this, but it is rejected, because what comes after *inna* does not operate on what comes before it.

The preferred view is the first, and stopping at *kadhalika* is complete.

Then the speech is resumed, and He (glory be to Him) informed us with His words: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾. Or it is part of His words: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18], with the meaning: only those who know Him fear Him (glory be to Him) unseen, and know what befits Him of His majestic attributes and beautiful acts. In every case, He (glory be to Him) has specified in this verse the people of His fear, and they are those who know Him and magnify His power.

Mujahid said: The scholar is only one who fears Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Masruq said: Fear of Allah is enough knowledge, and self-delusion is enough ignorance. Whoever knows Allah most, is most fearful of Him.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Whoever does not fear Allah is not a scholar.

Al-Sha'bi said: The scholar is one who fears Allah.

The reason for placing the object first (*ta'khir*, i.e. *taqdim al-maf'ul*) is that the context is a context of restricting the agency (*hasr al-fa'iliyyah*). If it were postponed, the matter would be reversed.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz read the noble name (Allah) in the nominative and *al-'ulama'* (the scholars) in the accusative, and this reading was narrated from Abu Hanifa. Al-Zamakhshari said in the *Kashshaf*: "Fear" in this reading is a metaphor, and the meaning is that He honours and magnifies them as a dreaded and awe-inspiring man is held in awe among people.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving﴾ is a reason for the obligation of fear, indicating that He punishes for disobedience to Him, and forgives whoever of His servants repents.

﴿Indeed those who recite the Book of Allah﴾, meaning they continue in its recitation and persist in it. The Book is the Noble Qur'an, and there is no basis for what is said, that what is meant by it is the category of the books of Allah. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning they perform it at its times with full pillars and remembrances. ﴿And spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. In this is an exhortation to spend in whatever way is possible: if it is possible secretly, that is better, and otherwise openly. Suspicion that it may be ostentation does not prevent it. It is possible that by secrecy is meant voluntary charity, and by openness obligatory charity.

The clause ﴿They hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ is in the place of nominative as the predicate of *inna*, as Tha'lab and others said. What is meant by commerce is the reward for obedience. The meaning of ﴿will never perish﴾ is will never become dull or be destroyed. It is a description of the commerce. The informing about their hope for the reward of what they did is in the position of a promise that their hoped-for thing will be attained.

The *lam* in ﴿that He may pay them their rewards﴾ is connected to ﴿will never perish﴾, with the meaning: that it will not become dull for the sake of paying them the rewards of their righteous deeds. A similar verse is His words (glory be to Him): ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nisa': 173]. It was also said that the *lam* is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, meaning: they did that so that He might pay them. The meaning of ﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾ is that He bestows upon them an increase beyond their rewards, which are the recompense for their deeds.

The clause ﴿Indeed He is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is a reason for what was mentioned of full payment and increase, meaning: He forgives their sins and appreciates their obedience. It was also said that this clause is the predicate of *inna*, and the clause ﴿they hope﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The first is preferable.

﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book﴾ refers to the Qur'an. It was also said it refers to the Preserved Tablet, with *min* being partitive or initial (indicating origin). The clause ﴿is the truth﴾ is the predicate of the relative pronoun. ﴿Confirming what is before it﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, meaning: agreeing with the books that came before it. ﴿Indeed Allah is, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾, meaning: encompassing all their affairs.

﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾. The first object of *awrathna* (We caused to inherit) is the relative pronoun, and the second object is *al-kitab* (the Book). The second object was placed first to honour and magnify the Book. The meaning is: "Then We caused those whom We chose from among Our servants to inherit the Book," which is the Qur'an. That is: We decreed and ordained that We would make the scholars of your community, O Muhammad, inherit this Book which We revealed to you. The meaning of their being chosen is their being selected and singled out. There is no doubt that the scholars of this community, from the Companions onward, have been honoured by Allah above all other servants. He made them a middle community so that they might be witnesses over mankind, and He honoured them by making them the community of the best of prophets and the master of the children of Adam (ﷺ).

Muqatil said: He means the Qur'an of Muhammad; We made it reach those whom We chose from among Our servants.

It was also said that the meaning is: We caused it to be inherited from the earlier nations, that is, We delayed it from them and gave it to those whom We chose. The first view is preferable.

Then He (glory be to Him) divided those whom He caused to inherit His Book and whom He chose from among His servants into three categories, so He said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾. Many people of knowledge have found the meaning of this verse problematic, because He (glory be to Him) made this category, the one who wrongs himself, part of that division, namely those whom He chose from among the servants. So how can one whom Allah has chosen be one who wrongs himself? It was said: the division refers to the servants, meaning: among Our servants is one who wrongs himself, and this is the disbeliever, and the pronoun in ﴿they will enter it﴾ refers to the moderate one and the foremost.

It was also said: What is meant by the one who wrongs himself is the one who falls short in acting upon it, and he is the one whose matter is deferred to Allah's command. It is not necessarily the case that the inheritors of the Book observe it with its full observance, because of His words: ﴿Then there succeeded them a later generation who inherited the Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]. This is open to question, because wronging oneself does not fit with being chosen.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who committed minor sins. This view has been narrated from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda' and 'A'isha. This is the preferred view, because committing minor sins does not contradict being chosen, nor does it prevent its doer from entering Paradise with those who enter it: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾, and so on to the end of what will come.

The sense in which he is one who wrongs himself is that he diminished his own reward by the minor sins he committed, which are forgiven for him. If he had done good deeds instead of those minor sins, he would have had a great share of reward for himself. It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who commits major sins.

The early scholars differed in explaining the foremost (*al-sabiq*) and the moderate (*al-muqtasid*). 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious one without qualification. This is also what al-Farra' said. Mujahid said in explaining the verse: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ refers to the companions of the left hand; ﴿and among them is one who is moderate﴾ refers to the companions of the right hand; ﴿and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ refers to the foremost of all people.

Al-Mubarrad said: the moderate is one who gives the world its due and the Hereafter its due.

Al-Hasan said: the one who wrongs himself is the one whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds; the moderate is the one whose good and evil deeds are equal; the foremost is the one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds.

Muqatil said: the one who wrongs himself is the people of major sins among the people of monotheism; the moderate is the one who has not committed a major sin; and the foremost is the one who hastened to righteous deeds.

Al-Nahhas reported that the one who wrongs himself is the owner of major sins, and the moderate is the one who did not deserve Paradise by having his good deeds outweigh his evil deeds, so the Gardens of Eden which they enter are for "those who hastened to good deeds" only. He said: This is the view of a group of people of reflection, because the pronoun in the true sense of reflection refers to what is nearest to it, which is preferable.

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, meaning: among their descendants is one who wrongs himself.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the foremost is the scholar, the moderate is the learner, and the one who wrongs himself is the ignorant.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who remembers Allah only with his tongue; the moderate is the one who remembers with his heart; and the foremost is the one who never forgets Him.

Al-Antaki said: the one who wrongs himself is the owner of words, the moderate is the owner of deeds, and the foremost is the owner of spiritual states.

Ibn 'Ata' said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who loves Allah for the sake of this world; the moderate is the one who loves Allah for the sake of the reward in the Hereafter; and the foremost is the one who let his own desire fall away in favour of the desire of the Truth.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who worships Allah out of fear of the Fire; the moderate is the one who worships Him out of hope for Paradise; and the foremost is the one who worships Him without any cause.

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who loves himself; the moderate is the one who loves his religion; and the foremost is the one who loves his Lord.

Some said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who takes his share (of the world) but does not give others their due. The moderate one (al-muqtasid) is the one who takes his share and gives others their due. The foremost (al-sabiq) is the one who gives others their due and does not take his share.

Al-Tha'labi and others have mentioned many sayings. There is no doubt that the linguistic meanings of "the wrongdoer" (al-zalim), "the moderate" (al-muqtasid) and "the foremost" (al-sabiq) are well known, and that the wrongdoer to himself is one who simply deprives himself of his benefit and loses what is better for him. So one who does not multiply acts of obedience has wronged himself in terms of the reward he has forfeited, even though he performs what Allah has made obligatory for him and avoids what Allah has forbidden. From this aspect, he is among those whom Allah has chosen and among the people of Paradise, so there is no difficulty in the verse. From this is the saying of Adam: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [Al-A'raf: 23], and the saying of Yunus: ﴿Indeed, I was among the wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 87]. The meaning of the moderate is one who takes a middle course in matters of religion, inclining neither to excess nor to negligence, and this one is among the people of Paradise. As for the foremost, he is the one who surpasses others in matters of religion, and he is the best of the three.

The placing of the wrongdoer before the moderate, and of both before the foremost, has been raised as a difficulty, given that the moderate is better than the wrongdoer to himself and the foremost is better than both. It was said that mention order does not necessarily imply honour, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal﴾ [Al-Hashr: 20], and similar Qur'anic verses in which the people of evil are mentioned before the people of good, and the less excellent are mentioned before the more excellent.

It was also said that the reason for the order here is that the moderate, in relation to the people of disobedience, are few, and the foremost, in relation to both groups, are fewer still; so the more numerous is placed before the less numerous. The first answer is preferable, for numerical abundance alone does not require earlier mention. Other reasons for the order have been given besides what we have mentioned, and there is no need to lengthen the discussion with them.

The reference in His saying "that" (dhalika) is to the inheritance of the Book and the choosing. It was said that it refers to the race to good deeds, but the first is preferable. It (dhalika) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "the great bounty", meaning the bounty whose extent cannot be measured.

The phrase ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is in the nominative either as a subject (mubtada') with what follows it as its predicate (khabar), or as an apposition (badal) to "the bounty", because it is the cause of attaining the reward and so has been treated as the one that causes it. On this view, the clause ﴿they will enter them﴾ is a new sentence (musta'nafah). We have already said that the pronoun in ﴿they will enter them﴾ refers to the three categories, so there is no basis for restricting it to the last category.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh and al-Tirmidhi read جَنَّةُ (jannah, singular). Al-Jahdari read جَنّاتٍ (jannatin) in the accusative, as an object construction (ishtighal). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that جَنّاتُ be a second predicate of the demonstrative. Abu 'Amr read يُدْخَلُونَها (yudkhalunaha) in the passive voice. The word يُحَلَّوْنَ (yuhallawna, "they will be adorned") is a second predicate of "Gardens of Eden", or a circumstantial clause (hal) that is understood. It derives from حَلِيَتِ المَرْأةُ (haliyati al-mar'ah, "the woman adorned herself with jewellery"). In it is an indication of speed of entry, for adorning them outside Paradise would delay their entry. So when He said يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيها ("they will be adorned therein"), He indicated that their entry will be swift. The "min" in مِن أساوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ: the first (min in "min asawira") is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the second (min in "min dhahab") is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: they will be adorned with some bracelets made of gold. Asawir is the plural of أسْوِرَة, the plural of siwar (bracelet). The accusative of لُؤْلُؤًا (lu'lu'an, "pearls") is by coordination with the position (mahall) of مِن أساوِرَ. It was also read in the genitive, coordinated with ذَهَبٍ. ﴿Their clothing therein is silk﴾: the interpretation of this verse has been fully given in Surah al-Hajj.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief"﴾. The majority read الحَزَنَ (al-hazan) with two fatahs. Jinah ibn Hubaysh read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay (al-huzn).

The meaning is that they will say this statement when they enter Paradise. Qatadah said: "Grief of death." 'Ikrimah said: "Grief over misdeeds and sins, and fear that their acts of obedience will be rejected." Al-Qasim said: "Grief over the loss of blessings and fear of the outcome." It was said: "Grief over the terrors of the Day of Resurrection." Al-Kalbi said: "What used to grieve them in the world concerning the matter of the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The concern for bread in this world." It was said: "The concern for livelihood."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Allah has removed from the people of Paradise all griefs, whether they were about livelihood or about the Hereafter."

This is the most preferred of the sayings, for the world, however great its pleasures, is not free of impurities and calamities, which cause many griefs, especially for the people of faith. They are always fearful of the punishment of Allah, afraid of His retribution, with hearts in turmoil at every moment, wondering: will their deeds be accepted or rejected? Fearful of the evil end and the bad conclusion. Then their concerns and griefs do not cease until they enter Paradise.

As for the people of disobedience: although their stranglehold may be loosened a little in the life of this world, which is the abode of delusion, and although they forget the abode of permanence for a time of their lives, their dread will certainly intensify and their calamity will grow, and the cauldrons of their griefs will boil when they approach death and draw near the abodes of the Hereafter. Then, when their souls are taken and what displeases them of the recompense for their deeds appears to them, their sorrow and grief increase. But if Allah bestows His favour upon them with forgiveness and admits them into Paradise, then He has removed their griefs and dispelled their sorrows and concerns. ﴿Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, meaning: Forgiving to whoever disobeys Him, and Appreciative to whoever obeys Him.

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty﴾, meaning the abode of residence in which one remains forever and from which one is never removed, by His grace and mercy. ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, meaning: no hardship, toil or difficulty will afflict us in Paradise. ﴿And no weariness touches us therein﴾: al-lughub is exhaustion from toil, and al-kalal is weariness from fatigue.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾: "White, red and black." And concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "White streaks," meaning colours.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "Gharabib (in His saying 'and jet-black') means the intensely black."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik, concerning His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾: "Streaks that exist in the mountain, white and red; these are the streaks." ﴿And jet-black﴾: "Black mountains." And concerning the people, the animals and the cattle he said: "Likewise is the diversity of people, animals and cattle, like the diversity of mountains." Then he said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "This is a separation from what precedes it."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the verse ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾: "The scholars of Allah, who fear Him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning the verse: "Those who know that Allah is capable of everything."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Adi related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Knowledge does not come from much narration; rather, knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tabarani related from him, who said: "Fear of Allah is sufficient as knowledge, and being deceived about Allah is sufficient as ignorance."

Ahmad in al-Zuhd also related from him: "Knowledge does not come from abundance of narration, but knowledge is fear (of Allah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Hudhayfah, who said: "It is enough for the believer of knowledge that he fears Allah."

'Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Thaqafi related in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas that Husayn ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn 'Abd Manaf was the one concerning whom ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah and establish prayer﴾ was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾: "They are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah made them inherit every Book that was revealed. So their wrongdoer to himself is forgiven, their moderate is held to a light account, and their foremost enters Paradise without reckoning."

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he "said concerning this verse: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ — he said: 'All of these are on one level, and all of them will enter Paradise.'" In its chain are two unknown men.

Imam Ahmad said in his Musnad: He said: "Shu'bah narrated to us from al-Walid ibn al-'Ayzar, that he heard a man from Thaqif narrating from a man from Kinanah, from Abu Sa'id."

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Abu al-Darda', who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants; among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by Allah's permission﴾. As for those who were foremost, they are the ones who enter Paradise without reckoning. As for those who were moderate, they will be held to a light account. As for those who wronged themselves, they will be detained for a long time at the gathering place, and then they are the ones whom Allah will overlook by His mercy. They are the ones who will say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ to the end of the verse.'"

Al-Bayhaqi said: "When narrations for a hadith multiply, it shows that the hadith has a basis." End of quote. In the chain of Ahmad is Muhammad ibn Ishaq. In the chain of Ibn Abi Hatim is an unknown man, for he narrated it through al-A'mash from a man, from Abu Thabit, from Abu al-Darda'. Ibn Jarir narrated it from al-A'mash, who said: "Abu Thabit mentioned it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from 'Awf ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "My Ummah is in three thirds: a third will enter Paradise without reckoning, a third will be held to a light account and then enter Paradise, and a third will be purified and examined, and then the angels will come and say: 'We found them saying: There is no god but Allah alone.' Allah will say: 'Admit them into Paradise because of their saying: There is no god but Allah alone, and place their sins upon the people of denial.' And these are what Allah refers to in His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 13]." And its confirmation is in what was mentioned concerning the angels.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾, and so He made them three groups.

﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾: this is the one who is examined and purified. ﴿And among them is one who is moderate﴾: this is the one who is held to a light account. ﴿And among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾: this is the one who enters Paradise without reckoning or punishment, by Allah's permission; they all enter it.

Ibn Kathir said after mentioning this hadith: "Very strange." End of quote.

Some of these hadiths strengthen one another, and they must be accepted. Through them the view of those who understood "the one who wrongs himself" as the disbeliever is refuted. They are supported by what al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Usamah ibn Zayd concerning ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "All of them are from this Ummah, and all of them are in Paradise." And by what al-Tayalisi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Uqbah ibn Sihban, who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What do you say about the saying of Allah: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾ and so on?' She said: 'As for the foremost, they are those who lived during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he testified for them to Paradise. As for the moderate, they are those who followed their traces and acted like their deeds until they joined them. As for the one who wrongs himself, he is like me and you, and whoever follows us, and all are in Paradise.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 3 of 3):
